  • Tools: list_collections, query_items (items service — RLS applies), aggregate (refuses when the user is row-filtered), semantic_search (hits intersected with the permission-checked read), integration_status (the obligation ledger for a record), record_event_path (the newest integration events naming a record and the path each set off — writes, transitions, flows, partner calls, where it failed), explain_access (why the asker — or, for administrators, another user — can or cannot see a record), record_integrity (a record's live integrity findings, or a collection's newest sweep totals) run_custom_query (a saved SQL query from the catalogue the assistant is given — only queries whose access admits the asker, User-Scope params injected, 200 rows at most) and queue_summary (a queue the asker may read, by name or id from the queue catalogue in the prompt: totals, by-state counts, SLA breaches with hours over and owners, the oldest and unowned records as friendly ids with links, and the at-risk rules firing most — read as the asker through the queue service, so scopes apply), waiting_on_me (the asker's own My Work “Waiting on you” list — records whose current pipeline step they own, SLA-breached first, plus approval steps naming them; no person parameter, narrowed to records the asker may read; an empty list is said as “nothing waiting”, never replaced by another list).
  • Ask about a queue from its page: the queue toolbar's "Ask about this queue" opens /ask with the question seeded (/ask?q=… seeds and sends one question, then drops the parameter).
  • Reads are direct; mutations only ever happen through the proposal gate (see AI Actions & Dashboards) — the model can never write without your approval.
  • Every answer shows the tool trace: exactly which queries produced it.
  • A breakdown or a series (per state, per month, per vendor) comes with a chart: the model attaches a fenced chart block ({type, title, data:[{label, value}]}) that renders as a bar, line or pie under the prose.
  • The same standalone question by the same person inside the answer-cache window (Settings → AI Features, default 15 minutes) answers from cache — the page says when it was first answered and offers "Ask again". Answers that propose an action are never cached; fresh: true in the request skips the cache.
  • An answer written only from the in-app docs (search_docs and no other tool, no page context, no remembered notes) is also kept for everyone: the next person asking the same question in the same language, with the same docs audience (administrators see more sections), gets it from cache. Any data tool keeps an answer private, and a new docs index never serves an answer quoting the old one.
  • Within one conversation, a read the assistant already made (same tool, same arguments, same person) is reused instead of queried again, as long as nothing in that collection changed since — the steps say "reused". A write in between, a configuration change, or 30 minutes passing makes it read again.
  • Tool results reach the model as compact tables (column names once, each link label once); Show the steps and exports keep the readable rows.
  • When an administrator switches on "Start cheap" for Ask AI (AI Quality → Cost savings), a quick answer from the smaller model says so and offers "Try harder", which asks the main model.
  • Under a single number (an ungrouped count, sum, average, minimum or maximum) the page offers "Tell me when this goes over…": pick a threshold (goes over, reaches, drops under, falls to) or a trend watch (alerts when the series changes direction or moves outside its recent range, using the anomaly engine statistics), and how often to check (daily or hourly). The watch is re-read hourly AS YOU, so permissions and row-level security apply; you get an in-app notification when it crosses (once per crossing, not every check). "Numbers you watch" at the top of /ask lists each with its current value, change today, threshold and last alert — edit the threshold, pause or stop watching. Watches live in your own account preferences (20 at most) via GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /api/ai/watches (POST /:id/check reads one now), and appear in your daily summary with the change since yesterday and whether they are close to the threshold. Ask "what am I watching" to have the assistant list them (my_watches).
  • The past_state tool reads revision and pipeline history under the same read gates as the revision API: "what did this record look like on March 1" (as_of), "when did the amount change and who changed it" (changes), "how long was it in Finance Review" (time_in_state).
  • Uses the chat model from Settings → AI Features → Model per feature; a model the gateway refuses falls back to the default model.
  • Answers stream as they are written: send stream: true and the route answers 202 {data: {stream_id}} at once, then emits ai:delta (text, with its round), ai:status (the tool running), ai:done (the full normal body — proposals, trace, request_id) and ai:error to your Socket.io user room; add Accept: text/event-stream to get the same events as SSE instead (widgets, hosts without the socket). A caller with neither gets the plain reply. POST /api/ai/chat/:stream_id/stop halts a running answer. /summarize and /generate take the same stream option with text deltas only. The /ask page streams by default, shows what the model is doing while tools run, and has a Stop button.

AI Knowledge

What Ask AI knows beyond the data itself: the in-app docs, a shared glossary of business terms and a data guide per collection. Admins manage it all on /ai/knowledge (Insights → AI → Knowledge); everyone else sees the glossary there.

Docs search

Ask AI has a search_docs tool over these Docs pages. For "how do I…" questions it quotes the passage and links the section (/docs?section=<id> opens this page there), next to the help-video search. Sections outside the Overview, User Guide and Collaboration groups are administrator material and are left out for people who are not administrators (a section can set its own audience). The search reads api/src/services/docs-index.json, regenerated by pnpm docs:ai-index and by pnpm sync-docs.

Glossary

  • A term has a definition, other spellings, an optional collection it belongs to, an optional rule ("is_on_hold = 1") and an optional saved query that computes the figure.
  • Ask AI uses the definitions and the same words in answers. A short glossary rides every prompt; a long one sends only the terms named in the question. A term scoped to a collection the asker cannot read is left out.
  • The app marks terms with a dotted underline and shows the definition on hover: on form field labels (terms scoped to another collection are skipped) and in Ask AI answers, where the first use of each term links to its entry.
  • Draft entries from the data: Suggestions → "Draft glossary from the data" proposes terms from choice lists, field help text and the docs. Nothing is added until an admin accepts (optionally edited) or dismisses it.

Data guides per collection

Hints and example questions for one collection ("forecasts are one row per workflow and year"), edited on the collection's Settings tab in the Data Model or on the Data guides tab. A guide is sent to Ask AI only when a question names the collection (or its display name, singular or plural) or closely matches one of its example questions, and rides list_collections for that collection — so the global guide in Settings → AI Features no longer has to hold everything.

Suggestions → "Draft guide lines from corrections" reads thumbs-down reasons (and any correction source an extension registers) and proposes guide lines, per collection or global, for an admin to accept, edit or dismiss.

Docs gaps

Every docs search that finds no section answering the question is logged. The Docs gaps tab groups those questions by topic with counts, people and examples — a list of docs to write. A topic drops off by itself once a docs section answers it; Dismiss removes it by hand. The "try" box runs the same search Ask AI uses.

Conflict check

The Conflicts tab lists glossary terms and data guides that work against each other: the same word defined two different ways, near-duplicate terms with different meanings, and terms or guides that name a collection, field or saved query that no longer exists. The check runs when you save a term or guide and every night at 03:45 (the nightly run also asks the AI to read the definitions for contradictions a word match cannot see). Each finding links to both sides. A finding resolves by itself when you fix the cause; Dismiss hides one you have decided to keep.

Topic map

The Topic map groups recent Ask AI questions by meaning and shows each topic by role: how many questions, how many went unanswered, how many got a thumbs-down and what they cost on average. A topic marked Gap goes wrong often and nothing in the glossary, data guides or playbooks matches its questions: write one. Topics have generated names; the questions themselves stay hidden unless you tick "Show sample questions", which is written to the activity log. Admins only.

Search index

Search by meaning only finds records that have been embedded. The Search index tab shows, per collection, how many records have no embedding yet or changed since their last one, how long the oldest of those has waited, and whether the embedding provider changed since the vectors were written (vectors from different providers cannot be compared, so the collection needs a reindex). Reindex embeds what is missing; after a provider switch it rebuilds every vector. A collection is flagged when a twentieth of its records are behind or a change has waited more than a day.

First-week checklists

On the First week tab pick a role and choose Draft with AI. The draft is built from what the role touches: its forms, the queues it can read, videos required of it and views shared with it, and every step points at something the role really has. Edit the steps, then Publish. Nothing reaches people until you do. A person whose role was set in the last two weeks sees the published list at the top of My Work; a step ticks itself when they open its link, finish its video or save a record in its collection, and they can hide the list. Redrafting never touches the published version.

GET    /api/ai-knowledge/glossary                 (everyone)
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/glossary                 (admin) {term, definition, aliases[], collection?, query_slug?, query_note?}
PATCH  /api/ai-knowledge/glossary/:id             (admin)
DELETE /api/ai-knowledge/glossary/:id             (admin)
GET    /api/ai-knowledge/data-guides[/:collection] (admin)
PUT    /api/ai-knowledge/data-guides/:collection  (admin) {hints, examples[]}
GET    /api/ai-knowledge/suggestions?status=      (admin)
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/suggestions/draft        (admin) {source: 'corrections' | 'data'}
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/suggestions/:id/accept   (admin) {payload?}
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/suggestions/:id/dismiss  (admin)
GET    /api/ai-knowledge/docs-gaps?days=          (admin)
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/docs-gaps/dismiss        (admin) {ids[]}
GET    /api/ai-knowledge/docs-search?q=           (signed in)
GET    /api/ai-knowledge/findings?status=         (admin)
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/findings/run             (admin) {ai?: boolean}
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/findings/:id/dismiss|reopen (admin)
GET    /api/ai-knowledge/topic-map?days=&questions= (admin)
GET    /api/search/freshness                      (admin)
POST   /api/search/reindex/:collection?force=1    (admin)
GET    /api/role-checklists[/:roleId]             (admin)
POST   /api/role-checklists/:roleId/draft|publish|unpublish (admin)
PUT    /api/role-checklists/:roleId               (admin) {steps[]}
GET    /api/my-work/first-week                    (signed in)

Ask AI history & sharing

Every Ask AI conversation is kept for the person who started it: each question, the answer, the tool calls behind it and any action it proposed (with that proposal’s outcome, read live). The History list beside the chat shows them newest first, pinned ones on top, and searches titles and text. Opening one resumes it — the next question goes to the model with the whole thread. The AI call log stays the administrator’s record; this history is the person’s own, and administrators get no view into it.

History, pins and retention

  • Pin a conversation from the list or the page header; pins sort first and are never pruned.
  • Delete removes the conversation and everything in it. Someone it was shared with can remove it from their own list instead. Deleting a single message deletes your own; the owner removing someone else’s message only empties it — it stays a withheld turn, so later answers that may repeat it stay withheld too.
  • Settings → AI Features → Ask AI conversation history: how many days an untouched conversation is kept (blank = 180, 0 = forever). The nightly retention job prunes the rest, except conversations any participant has pinned.

Don’t save my questions

Each person can turn Ask AI history off — Profile → Ask AI history, or the switch at the top of the History list on the Ask page. From then on nothing they ask is stored as a conversation: answers still work live (the thread lives in the open page only), but there is no History entry, and Share, Post to chat, Branch, export and saved plan cards are unavailable because they need a saved conversation. A saved conversation opened while history is off is read-only. Turning it on offers a separate “Also delete my saved conversations” — it deletes only the conversations that person started (with their shares to other people); conversations others shared with them stay.

Still kept while history is offWhat and for how long
Ask AI memory notesOnly the notes the person explicitly saved; they edit or delete them on Profile.
Thumbs up/downOnly when the person chooses to give one: the rating and any comment they type, kept in the AI feedback table.
AI call log (administrators)One row per model call with tokens, cost, latency and capped copies of the request and response — which include the question — pruned after 30 days. Visible to administrators in AI analytics. Unchanged by this switch.
Activity logAn ai-chat entry per question with the number of tool calls — no question text.
Answer cacheThe same standalone question by the same person answers from a per-person Redis cache for the configured window (default 15 minutes), then expires.
Not keptThe conversation itself, and the shared playbook of worked examples (a question asked with history off never becomes one).

Ask AI memory

Say “remember that amounts are in thousands” (or “remember: I work Zone 3 inventory requests”) and Ask AI keeps the note instead of answering. Notes ride every later question as context about you. Profile → Ask AI memory lists them for editing or deleting. At most 20 notes of 300 characters; when the list is full a new note is refused — nothing is ever dropped to make room — and the answer links to Profile → Ask AI memory to remove one first. Notes are stored in your preferences and never grant access to anything. Nobody else writes them — administrators included: they are left out of user reads, lists and revisions, and an administrator’s edit of your preferences keeps your notes as they were.

Remember this? When a question shows a lasting preference (“by my zone I mean Zone 3”, “show amounts in thousands”), Ask AI may offer a note under its answer. Nothing is kept unless you click Remember; “Not now” hides the offer. Offers are only ever shown to the person who asked — never to someone a conversation is shared with — and are never offered for one-off facts, record values, other people or anything that reads as an instruction to Ask AI (“call…”, “ignore…”, “always run…”). The offer says plainly that the note is added to every future question. With Ask AI history off, offers still appear and Remember keeps only the note. At most two per answer, none once your memory is full (a click on a full list is refused the same way, with a link to Profile).

Administrators can view and clear a person’s notes for a support or compliance request: People → the person → Admin tools → Ask AI memory. The notes stay hidden until Show notes; each view and each clear (one note or all) is written to the activity log as ai-memory-view / ai-memory-clear with counts only. Administrators can remove notes but never add or reword them.

Sharing a conversation

The owner shares a conversation with colleagues (Share in the header). They are notified, see it in their History, can read it and can ask follow-ups in the same thread; a new question or answer appears for everyone who has it open. Each person’s questions run with their own permissions.

An answer is shown to someone other than the person it was asked for only when it is safe to: it made at least one data call, every call is a plain read (not saved SQL, not an action proposal) that did not error, re-running each one with the reader’s access returns exactly what the model saw, and every earlier answer in the thread is readable by the reader too (the model saw those answers and may repeat them). Otherwise — including an answer with no data calls, or data that has changed since — the answer is withheld from that reader with an “Ask it with my access” button. Opening a thread re-checks at most 10 calls; anything past that is withheld until asked again. A follow-up asked by the reader is built only from the turns they may read.

Live sessions: while one person’s answer streams, everyone else with the thread open follows it — each finished step, then the answer text — but only once every step so far has been re-run with their own access and returned exactly what the model saw, and every earlier answer is readable by them. Text written before any data call, a step that is not a plain read, or a result that differs for them stops the stream for that person: they see that someone is asking, then the answer when it is stored, under the rule above.

Ask in the background

The clock button next to Send asks the question in the background: a longer run with a bigger budget of data calls, shown in the Jobs tray while it works. It reads with your access, and it can only read — it cannot draft changes or plans (ask on the page for those). The answer is saved to the conversation in your Ask history and you get an inbox notification; Cancel in the tray or under the question stops it and keeps whatever had arrived. It needs your Ask history on, and at most two run at once.

Branching

Hover an earlier question and choose Edit to ask a different version of it. The answer continues in a new conversation (a branch) that holds everything before the edited question as you could read it — an answer withheld from you is copied as an empty placeholder that still counts as withheld; the original thread stays as it was. History nests branches under their source, and the conversation page links between them.

Posting to chat

The owner can Post to chat: it sends the conversation to a channel, direct message or record room as a card: the question, a short answer and an Open link. The card is built for each reader — the short answer appears only when the sharing rule above admits them; otherwise it says the answer was given with the poster’s access. Anyone who can read the room can open the conversation and ask follow-ups with their own access.

Export and formats

  • An answer built from a query offers CSV and Excel. The download re-runs the query with your access today — it never copies the answer’s text — and is named after the question and the time.
  • A table, chart or “label: value” list in an answer has a Table · Chart · List switch. The other formats are drawn from the same rows, with no new question and no model call. A chart needs a column of numbers.
  • Add to dashboard (under a chart answer) keeps the chart on one of your dashboards, or a new one. The widget stores the query behind the chart — the grouped count or total, or the saved query — not the answer, and re-runs it with the access of whoever views the dashboard. Hover its title to see the question it came from.
  • Copy as code (administrators, and people with an API token or key) turns the reads an answer made into an SDK call, a REST request and a curl command. Anything naming data you cannot see — a filter on a hidden field, a grouping, a saved query you may not run — is left out and counted.

API

RouteWhat it does
POST /api/ai/chat { messages, save: true }Ask and start a stored conversation. The answer carries conversation_id.
POST /api/ai/chat { messages, conversation_id }Ask inside a conversation. The server builds the history from the turns the caller may read; only the newest question in messages is used.
POST /api/ai/memory { text }Keep a note the answer offered (memory_suggestions on the answer) in the caller’s own memory. 409 when the memory is full.
GET /api/users/:id/ai-memoryAdministrators: a person’s notes. Logged as ai-memory-view.
DELETE /api/users/:id/ai-memory[/:noteId]Administrators: clear all notes, or one. Logged as ai-memory-clear.
GET /api/ai/conversations?q=&pinned=1Mine and shared with me, newest first.
GET /api/ai/conversations/:idThe thread as the caller may read it (visible: false = withheld), shares (owner only), branches, parent.
PATCH /api/ai/conversations/:id { title?, pinned? }Rename (owner) or pin (each person their own).
DELETE /api/ai/conversations/:idOwner: delete. Shared: remove from my list.
DELETE /api/ai/conversations/mineDelete every conversation the caller started (with its shares). PATCH /api/users/me/preferences { ai_history_off: true | null } is the opt-out; with it on, save is ignored and conversation_id answers 409.
POST /api/ai/conversations/:id/shares { user_ids }Owner shares with people (notifies them).
DELETE /api/ai/conversations/:id/shares/:shareIdOwner stops sharing.
POST /api/ai/conversations/:id/branch { message_id, question }New conversation holding the turns before that question; ask question in it next.
POST /api/ai/conversations/:id/post { room, note? }Owner only: post to a chat room they can see.
GET /api/ai/conversations/:id/messages/:mid/export?format=csv|xlsx&step=The rows behind an answer, re-run as the caller.
DELETE /api/ai/conversations/:id/messages/:midRemove one message (owner, or your own).
POST /api/ai/research { question, conversation_id? }Ask in the background (202 {run_id, conversation_id, question_message_id}); 409 with history off, 429 past two running.
POST /api/ai/research/:run/cancelStop a background question (its asker, or an admin).
GET /api/ai/answer-code?conversation_id=&message_id=An answer’s reads as {snippets: [{title, sdk, rest, curl, omitted}], skipped} for the caller; GET /api/ai/answer-code/access says whether they may.

Live updates: participants receive ai:conversation {conversation_id, by, message_id, state: asking|answered|failed} on their user room — ids only; the client refetches and the server filters the answer per reader. A live answer arrives as ai:live {conversation_id, message_id, by: {id, name}, kind: working|step|delta|end, tool?, summary?, text?, round?} — steps and text only for readers the checks above admit.

Ask AI panel shortcuts

Everything here runs as you: starter questions name only what you can open, saved views are the ones you can see, and every figure or row is read with your own permissions, row rules and scopes. None of it adds a model call beyond the answer itself.

Starter questions and follow-ups

The empty chat offers two or three questions fitted to the page it was opened from — “Why is workflows #12 late?” on a record you can open, “Which records in queue 7 breach their SLA today?” on a queue, “What changed since last month?” on a report — plus the examples an administrator wrote into the collection’s data guide. After each answer, three short next questions drawn from what the tools found appear under it; one click asks one. They are written in the same call as the answer.

Slash commands

Type / in the Ask box to list the commands, then Tab or Enter to pick one.

CommandWhat it does
/chart <question>Answers with a chart (bar, line or pie) built from the numbers the tools return.
/table <question>Answers as a table.
/explainExplains how the last answer was reached: what was read, how the figure was computed, access limits.
/steps <question>Answers as a short numbered list of steps.
/export [xlsx]Downloads the last answer’s rows as CSV (or Excel), re-run with your access.

Clarifying questions

When a question is genuinely ambiguous (“which zone?”, “this year or the funding year?”) and no sensible default exists, the answer asks with clickable options instead of guessing: the distinct values of a column, matching records you can read, or short interpretations. Picking one continues the same conversation. Answers that ask a question are never cached or shared as replayable.

Saved views by name

Say “my late IRs view” and Ask AI resolves it to a saved view you can see — your own, ones shared with everyone, and ones shared with your role. The view’s filter is checked against the fields you may read (a view that filters on a hidden field is refused, not trimmed) and its rows are read as you. The filter can then be extended or grouped by a follow-up question.

Comparing

Ask for “Q1 vs Q2 spend by zone”, “this year vs last year” or “compare these two requests”. The compare tool runs the same guarded aggregate over both sets and returns values with deltas (B minus A, and percent), or lays two to four records side by side with the differing fields first. Fields you cannot read are never shown.

Drilling into a chart

Click a bar, point or slice of a chart answer to open the rows behind it in a sheet. The grouping is re-run as you and matched to the point you clicked; Open as list takes you to the collection filtered to exactly those records (up to 500).

Live answers

A number or chart answer that was built only from counts and sums stays current while you leave it open: when records in its collection change, the same aggregate is re-run as you (debounced, no model call) and the fresh figure appears under the answer, marked “updated …”. Updates stop while the tab is hidden and when you pause or close the answer. Only the newest two such answers refresh.

API

GET  /api/ai/starters?page=&collection=&id=     (signed in) starter questions for a screen
POST /api/ai/chat                               body.command = chart | table | explain | steps
POST /api/ai/chart-drill {collection, group_by, filter?, label}   (signed in) rows behind a chart point
POST /api/ai/live-answer {input: {collection, op, field?, group_by?, filter?}}   (signed in) re-run one aggregate

AI Actions & Dashboards

Ask AI can propose mutations — never execute them directly. Every proposal is stored, previewed in an approval card, and only runs when the proposing user clicks Approve within one hour.

Action types

  • bulk_update — a filter plus field changes; affected records resolve through the permission-checked read path (RLS applies), capped at 200.
  • create_record — a single new record from field values.
  • create_dashboard — a named dashboard with up to 12 widgets (count, sum, avg, latest, bar_chart, line_chart); widget collections need read permission and fields validate against the registry.
POST /api/ai/proposals/:id/approve   → executes as the proposer
POST /api/ai/proposals/:id/reject    → discards

Execution goes through the items service per row — hooks, validation,
row security, computed fields and activity logging all run.
Proposals expire after one hour and can only be approved by the user who asked. Dashboards are created private to the proposer.

Multi-step Plans

A request that needs several changes together — "close out the lines on these 12 POs and tell their owners" — comes back from Ask AI as one numbered plan instead of separate proposals. Each step carries its own preview, built as you when the plan is proposed; nothing runs until you approve.

  • Approve & run all runs every step in order; Run next step runs one and pauses, so you can approve step by step. Every step runs as you through the normal services — permissions, row security, validation, hooks and activity all apply.
  • Step kinds: update records (bulk_update), create a record, create a task, create a dashboard, send a message (an in-app notification to named people and/or the current owners of records — owners are resolved again when the step runs), post to a chat room you can see, and run an active manual flow (administrators only).
  • A refused step stops the plan with the reason; the steps after it stay pending. A bulk step where some records refuse reports how many and which.
  • Conditions: a step can say "only if still in Finance Review" (a filter the records must still match) or "only if the amount is unchanged" (fields that must still hold the value they had when the plan was made). A step whose condition fails is skipped and named in the result; on a bulk update only the records that fail are left out and the rest run.
  • While a plan runs, the card shows each step start, finish, fail or skip as it happens, with a running count of records changed.
  • Retry: after fixing the cause, Re-check and retry rebuilds the failed step and the ones after it as you now — a bulk step re-reads its filter and, after a partial run, keeps only the records that refused — shows which steps changed, then runs from where the plan stopped.
  • While an answer is being built, each tool step is listed as a plain line ("Reading workflows… 42 found") above the answer and folds away once the answer starts.
  • A plan nobody started expires after an hour, like a single proposal.

API

GET  /api/ai/plans/step-kinds     the step kinds the model may use
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id            the plan with each step's state (owner or administrator)
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/run        {mode: "all" | "next"} → 202; steps run in the background
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/retry      re-check the failed + remaining steps → status paused
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/cancel     discard, or stop a running plan before its next step

The chat answer carries proposed plans in plans next to proposals. Progress is pushed to your Socket.io user room as ai:plan ({plan_id, status, records_changed, step, plan}); ai:status events of a streamed answer now also arrive with done: true and a short result when each tool returns. Plans are stored in nivaro_ai_proposals with action_type plan.

Impact and change report

Every plan card leads with its impact, read off the step previews: "Touches 34 records in 3 collections, messages 12 people, moves 5 records to Approved". "What changes" opens the change report — every field the plan would change (or, for steps that ran, did change), per record, old value → new value — with an Excel download. The report is built for whoever looks at it: a record you cannot read shows as #id with no values, a field you cannot read as (hidden).

Run later

"Run later…" approves the plan for a set time. Each minute the ai-plans-scheduled job picks up the due plans; before running, every pending step is rebuilt as you at that moment. If the records a step would act on changed, or a step no longer builds, nothing runs: the plan comes back to you for approval with the new previews and the reason, and you get a notification. Cancel the schedule from the card to approve it again by hand.

When a plan finishes, the person who approved it gets a notification (in-app, plus push or Teams by their own notification rules) with the outcome, the failed step if any, and a link to the plan.

Plan history, undo and templates

  • /ai-plans (Home → AI Plans) lists plans with who approved them and when, their steps, impact and outcome. Everyone sees their own; administrators see every plan.
  • Undo (administrators): a step that wrote records can be reverted record by record, but only where nothing has changed the record since — its newest revision is still the plan's write and every field still holds the value the plan wrote. Records changed since are named and left alone. Messages, chat posts, flows and tasks cannot be undone.
  • Make a draft flow (administrators, plans that ran to the end): the steps become flow operations, chained in order, with the records as the same ids, the original filter, or whichever record fired an update event. The flow is created switched off and opens in the tester. Record updates and creates use the new Write Records flow operation, which runs as whoever triggered the flow through the normal record rules. When nobody triggers it (a webhook, a schedule, a system event) it runs only as a 'Run as' person named on the operation — never as the flow's author — and refuses without one; that person must be active, and the collection must be named, not templated.
  • Templates: ready-made plans for common chores (close out a record's open lines, reassign a leaver's open records, move old drafts to a status, tell the owners of matching records). Fill in the blanks and the usual plan preview appears; nothing runs until you approve. Administrators add their own (blanks + steps as JSON).
  • Data Integrity: on a run's field + rule filter, "Fix as a plan…" builds the confident fixes for that cluster as a plan, previewed record by record in the change report before approval.
GET  /api/ai/plans?scope=mine|all&status=
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id/changes          (+ /changes.xlsx)
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/schedule         {"run_at": "2026-10-16T21:00:00Z"}
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/unschedule
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id/undo             administrators
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/undo             {"step_id"?: "…"}  administrators
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/flow             {"records": "same"|"filter"|"trigger"}  administrators
GET  /api/ai/plan-templates
POST /api/ai/plan-templates/propose     {"key": "old-drafts", "values": {…}}
POST /api/config-conformance/runs/:id/plan  {"field", "rule"}  administrators

AI Features

Nivaro includes Claude-powered AI features for content generation and record summarization. AI features are admin-only and require an Anthropic API key. The key can be configured in two ways: set the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable on the server, or enter it in Settings → AI Features → Anthropic API Key. The settings value takes precedence when the env var is absent. When no key is found, all AI endpoints return 503 Service Unavailable.

FeatureWhereDescription
Generate with AIItem editor — field labelGenerates a value for a text/string field using the record's existing data as context.
SummarizeItem editor — page headerProduces a 2-3 sentence plain-English summary of the full record for a business user.
AI features are available to admin users only. The "AI" button on fields and the "Summarize" button in the header are hidden for non-admin users.

Per-person limits and timeouts

# .env — all optional
AI_USER_CALLS_PER_MINUTE=120     # AI calls one person may make per minute (per process); 0 = off
AI_USER_DAILY_TOKENS=10000000    # tokens one person may use per day (from nivaro_ai_calls); 0 = off
AI_CALL_TIMEOUT_MS=60000         # per call; grows with max_tokens, capped at 5 minutes
AI_CHAT_DEADLINE_MS=240000       # Ask AI wraps up after this (background research: 20 minutes)
AI_VALIDATION_HARD_FAIL=open     # hard-mode AI validation lets saves through when the check cannot run
AI_SPLIT_SYSTEM=off              # one system block instead of a cached stable part + per-question tail
EMBEDDING_SCAN_MAX=20000         # newest vectors semantic search ranks over

Over a limit the call answers 429 AI_RATE_LIMITED or AI_DAILY_TOKENS. Calls with no person behind them (scheduled jobs) are never limited. Hard-mode AI validation refuses the save with 503 AI_VALIDATION_UNAVAILABLE when the check cannot run, unless AI_VALIDATION_HARD_FAIL=open.

Generate with AI

On the item edit page, text and string fields show a small ✦ AI button next to the field label. Clicking it calls POST /api/ai/generate with the current collection, item ID, and field name. Claude reads the full record and writes a suggested value directly into the field — you can edit or discard it before saving.

API

POST /api/ai/generate
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "collection": "articles",
  "item_id": "123",
  "field": "summary",
  "context": "Optional extra instructions for the AI"
}

→ 200 { "data": { "value": "Generated field content..." } }
→ 400 { "error": "collection, item_id, and field are required" }
→ 404 { "error": "Item not found" }
→ 503 { "error": "AI features require ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to be configured" }

Model

Uses claude-haiku-4-5 with max_tokens: 500. The prompt includes the full record JSON, field metadata (note/description if present), and any additional context you provide.

Summarize

The Summarize button in the item editor header calls POST /api/ai/summarize. The result appears in a dismissible amber info box below the header — it is not saved to the record.

API

POST /api/ai/summarize
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "collection": "inventory_requests",
  "item_id": "456"
}

→ 200 { "data": { "summary": "This inventory request..." } }
→ 400 { "error": "collection and item_id are required" }
→ 404 { "error": "Item not found" }
→ 503 { "error": "AI features require ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to be configured" }

Model

Uses claude-haiku-4-5 with max_tokens: 200. The prompt instructs the model to produce a 2-3 sentence plain-English summary for a business user.

Server configuration

# .env
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
The server starts normally without ANTHROPIC_API_KEY — the field is optional. AI endpoints return 503 until the key is provided.

AI Review & Brief

Two authenticated (not admin-only) AI endpoints for headless frontends: POST /api/ai/review runs a pre-submission review of a record and returns a findings list, and POST /api/ai/brief renders a short plain-text briefing from context the caller supplies.

Record review

Reviews a record plus up to three of its one-to-many child sets (line items ride along automatically). If the collection has plain-text AI validation rules configured (AI Collection Settings), they are folded into the review guidance. The caller must have read permission on the collection; nivaro_* collections are rejected.

POST /api/ai/review
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "collection": "workflows", "item": "123" }

→ 200 { "data": { "findings": [
    { "severity": "error",      "field": "lines",       "message": "Line 3 has a quantity of 0." },
    { "severity": "warning",    "field": "date_required", "message": "Required date is in the past." },
    { "severity": "suggestion", "field": "description", "message": "Description looks like placeholder text." }
  ] } }
→ 400 { "error": "collection and item are required" }   // or "Invalid collection"
→ 403 { "error": "Forbidden" }                          // no read permission
→ 404 { "error": "Item not found" }
→ 503 { "error": "AI features require ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to be configured" }

Severity is always one of error / warning / suggestion; an empty findings array means the record looks ready to submit. Each call is activity-logged as ai-review.

Briefing

The caller gathers the data (custom queries, aggregates, anything) and sends it as one text block — the endpoint only writes the words. The prompt that writes it is chosen on the server from a fixed list — pass template: daily (the default: one-sentence opener, 3-5 concrete insights citing real numbers, immediate-attention callouts, one or two positives, plain text, 150-220 words), report-compare, report-explain or traffic-spike. Custom instructions are ignored (the answer carries instructions_ignored: true); the context is treated as data, never as instructions. Each person may run 2 briefs at once and 10 a minute (429 beyond).

POST /api/ai/brief
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "context": "User: Jane (admin). Today: Mon Aug 3.\n\nActive workflows (25 rows): [...]\nBudget health: [...]",
  "template": "daily"
}

→ 200 { "data": { "brief": "Good morning — three workflows need attention today..." } }
→ 400 { "error": "context is required" }
→ 429 { "error": "Too many briefs at once" }
→ 502 { "error": "The AI provider did not answer" }
→ 503 { "error": "AI features require ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to be configured" }
Context is capped at 16,000 characters and the response at 512 tokens. Responses are not cached server-side — callers that want a once-per-day briefing should cache client-side.

Fill a record from a document

A new-record form can read a statement of work, a quote, a purchase order PDF, a spreadsheet or an email and propose the whole record — header fields, related records, line items, a schedule — for a person to review before anything is saved. Off by default; turned on per collection.

Turning it on

  • Data Model → the collection → Settings → AI Features → **Fill from document**. The new-record form of that collection gains a "Fill from document" button beside "Import from file".
  • Settings → AI Features → **Model per feature** → *Document autofill* (gateway provider only). Blank uses the Ask AI model. This is a multi-step tool loop — the model looks vendors, people and categories up, then hands back a structured proposal — so it wants the strong model, not the one-shot one. A model the gateway refuses falls back to the chat model, then the default.
  • Same card, under the switch: **Hints for the reader** (plain sentences the model reads before every document of this collection), **keyed hints** (added once a named field resolves to a record whose label contains a text — a vendor's quirks), and the **confidence needed to fill a field** (default 40%, per-field overrides). A value under its threshold is offered as an ask with the candidate, never filled.
  • AI governance: the feature key is extract-record; disabling it in ai_disabled_features hides the button everywhere.

Three ways in

  • **Fill from document** on the new-record form — pick one document or several at once (a statement of work and its quote): they are read together as one record, every file is attached, and each source names the document it came from. **Add another document…** in the review reads one more beside the ones already stored. The run goes to the server at once; the dialog shows what it is doing and offers **Tell me when it's ready** — the dialog folds into a small chip in the corner that follows you across pages, keeps reading, and turns into a Review button when the proposal lands; close the tab, and a notification opens the form on it instead.
  • **Still needs you** — a relation ask's picker narrows the way the form's own picker would: by the field's cascade rules over what the proposal is keeping (a Project ask offers the projects of the proposed zone, region and type) and by its option filter, and it follows the other asks as you answer them.
  • **New from document…** in a list's "+ New item" menu (and the portal's + New menu): pick the file first, land on the new form with the review dialog open (?autofill=<proposal id>, kept 24 hours).
  • **Fill from document** on a new addendum: the proposal is built against the addendum layout's fields and lines.

What happens

  • The file is read to plain text (PDF via poppler when installed, else in process; DOCX; XLSX/CSV sheets; text, HTML, .eml). Scanned PDFs with no text layer are refused with a clear message — nothing is invented from an image.
  • The model sees the collection's fillable fields from its active layout (types, choices, notes), its child collections (lines, materials, schedules) and its multi-select relations. Small lookup tables (types, regions, years — up to 200 rows) are listed whole; big ones (vendors, people, locations, items) are searched through search_records, which runs the same permission-checked read the person could do by hand.
  • The proposal comes back as one structured call: value, confidence and the sentence it came from, per field and per line, plus "asks" for anything the document does not say.
  • The form's dependencies are honoured: a field narrowed by others (a project under a zone and a project type) is searched WITH those parents once they are settled, and a value the picker would not offer becomes an ask that names the parent excluding it. Cross-record defaults and field rules then fill what the document did not cover (a project's zones, regions and funding years; a rule's derived value) — shown with a "default" / "rule" pill; the document always wins.
  • A document past the prompt cap is condensed: the head is read whole, every later part is read once for verbatim passages that could fill a field, and those excerpts join the run (the dialog says how many parts were read).
  • The review dialog lists fields, lines, links and asks with checkboxes and confidence pills. An ask can be answered in place — a record picker for a relation, a choice list, a date — and a refused candidate is one click away. Apply STAGES the selection exactly like an import prefill — lines run the grid's row rules, the document attaches to the record's file field — and the record still needs Create.
  • What people keep, change before Create or answer is recorded per proposal: the AI Analytics page shows a scorecard per collection and per field, and the last corrections ride the next extraction's prompt as worked examples.

What keeps it honest

  • A relation id is accepted only when it came back from a lookup in that same request, or is one of the listed options. Anything else becomes an ask, never a silent guess.
  • Choices must match a configured choice; dates are normalised to ISO; numbers must parse; a one-line text field never receives a paragraph.
  • Line amounts are summed and compared with any total the model set on the parent; a mismatch is shown as a warning.
  • Required fields the document never covered are listed under "Still needs you".
  • Every run is activity-logged (ai-extract) and every model call lands in AI Analytics under feature extract-record.

API

GET  /api/ai/extract-record/config/:collection      → { data: { enabled, accept: [".pdf", …] } }
POST /api/ai/extract-record   multipart: collection=<name>, file=<upload>, layout_id?=<addendum layout>, background?=1
→ 200 { data: { id, summary, fields[{…, derived?}], children[], m2m[], asks[{…, candidate?, input?}], warnings[], prefill, document, model, rounds, latency_ms, condensed?, hints_used[] } }
→ 202 { data: { proposal_id, status: "running" } }   (background=1)
→ 403 feature off / collection not enabled / no create permission
→ 413 over 25 MB · 422 no readable text · 502 the model returned no proposal
GET  /api/ai/extract-record/result/:id          → the stored proposal (202 while running, 422 when it failed; kept 24 h)
POST /api/ai/extract-record/:id/notify          → tell the asker when a running proposal lands
POST /api/ai/extract-record/:id/apply           { kept_fields[], kept_lines, resolved_asks[] }   (the review dialog's Apply)
POST /api/ai/extract-record/:id/outcome         { record_id, values }   (which proposed values changed before Create)
GET  /api/ai/extract-record/analytics?days=     → the scorecard (admin)
Cost: a 5-page SOW on Sonnet is roughly 4–6 model rounds, 50–70 seconds, a few tens of cents. The system prompt (field spec + option lists) is prompt-cached across the rounds.

AI Content Validation

AI content validation checks items against natural-language rules before they are saved. Rules are written in plain English per collection ("the title must not contain pricing information", "the summary must be in a professional tone") and evaluated by Claude against the submitted values. Each rule is either soft (warn) or hard (block).

Managing in the admin UI

Open Data Model → select a table → Settings tab → "AI Features" card. Add validation rules as plain-text statements and choose Warn or Block per rule. Settings are stored per collection in nivaro_ai_collection_settings. In the item editor, violations of soft rules appear as inline warnings next to the affected fields — the save still goes through. Hard rules block the save.

Soft warn vs hard block

ModeItem editorAPI behaviour
Soft (warn)Inline warning banner per violated rule; user may save anyway.Save succeeds; violations are returned for display only.
Hard (block)Save is prevented until the content passes or the rule is changed.Create/update is rejected with 422 Unprocessable Entity listing the violated rules.

API

POST /api/ai/validate
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "collection": "articles",
  "data": { "title": "Cheap deal — only $9.99!", "body": "..." }
}

→ {
  "data": {
    "valid": false,
    "violations": [
      {
        "rule": "The title must not contain pricing information",
        "severity": "block",
        "explanation": "The title mentions a specific price ($9.99)."
      }
    ]
  }
}
Hard rules are also enforced server-side via a before-create/before-update hook — direct API writes that violate a blocking rule receive a 422 regardless of which client sent them. Requires an Anthropic API key (env or Settings → AI Features); without a key, validation is skipped entirely.

Aggregate cap rules (sum_cap)

A sum_cap rule caps the running SUM of a numeric field across rows sharing a group value against a limit read from a related parent record — e.g. "the sum of allocated_amount across all workflows for a unit must not exceed that unit's total_budget". It lives in the SAME validation_rules array as the plain-text AI rules above (a typed object instead of a string), evaluated by its own hook rather than by Claude — no API key needed.

Add one from Data Model → table → Settings tab → "AI Features" card → Rules → Sum Cap (next to AI Prompt). Configure: Sum field (the numeric column being summed), Group by (an M2O field on this collection — rows are grouped by its value), Cap relation (usually the same M2O field, resolved to the parent collection) and Cap field (the numeric field on that parent holding the limit), a Block/Warn severity, and a Message shown to the editor when the cap is exceeded.

{
  "type": "sum_cap",
  "severity": "block",
  "sum_field": "allocated_amount",
  "group_by": "unit_id",
  "cap": { "relation": "unit_id", "field": "total_budget" },
  "message": "Allocations would exceed the unit's budget"
}

On create/update, the hook sums sum_field across every other row with the same group_by value, adds the incoming write's own value, and compares against cap.field on the parent found by following cap.relation (an M2O field) to its related collection. block throws a 422 and lets the write through only if the total stays under the cap; warn sends the acting user an in-app notification and lets the write through regardless.

PATCH /api/units/abc123
{ "allocated_amount": 5000 }

→ 422 {
  "statusCode": 422,
  "error": "Unprocessable Entity",
  "message": "Aggregate cap exceeded: Allocations would exceed the unit's budget (18000 exceeds cap of 15000)",
  "code": "VALIDATION_CAP_EXCEEDED",
  "violations": [
    { "rule": "sum_cap", "field": "allocated_amount", "explanation": "Allocations would exceed the unit's budget (18000 exceeds cap of 15000)" }
  ]
}
This is the SAME error envelope shape a hard AI validation rule produces on a blocked write (code: "AI_VALIDATION_FAILED" there instead) — both are before-hook errors carrying a statusCode that the hook registry rethrows instead of swallowing, and server.ts's global error handler attaches code/violations onto the response whenever both are present on the thrown error. The one difference: an AI violation has no field key (the rule is free text), while a sum_cap violation always does.
sum_cap has known limitations, by design: (1) the check is lock-free — two concurrent writes to the same group can each individually pass the check and jointly exceed the cap (TOCTOU). (2) The SUM is computed under the CALLER's own row-level-security/workspace scope, matching how the rest of the write path scopes reads — under a row-filtered role the cap is effectively enforced per-visible-rows, not across the whole group. (3) Like the AI-validation hook, this hook fails OPEN on any non-HTTP error (a transient DB error skips the check rather than blocking the write) — only errors that carry an explicit statusCode (i.e. the cap itself firing) block. (4) A NULL group value or a NULL/missing cap on the parent both skip the check silently rather than erroring. (5) The cap lookup assumes group_by IS the FK named by cap.relation — it reads the group value straight off the child row and looks it up as the parent's id. A rule where the two name different fields caps against the wrong (or nonexistent) parent and, per (4), skips silently rather than erroring.
The admin PATCH endpoint (PATCH /api/ai-settings/:collection) preserves plain-text rule strings as-is but validates every typed rule object against the full sum_cap shape on save — a malformed or garbage object in the array is silently dropped rather than coerced (this used to render as the literal string "[object Object]" before the fix). The GET side is deliberately more lenient, so a rule that no longer validates still displays in the editor for the admin to fix or remove instead of vanishing.

AI Duplicate Detection

Duplicate detection warns users before they create a record that looks like an existing one. The new record's text fields are embedded into a vector and compared against existing records by cosine similarity — semantically similar records ("Acme Corp." vs "ACME Corporation Inc.") are caught even when no keyword matches.

Managing in the admin UI

Open Data Model → select a table → Settings tab → "AI Features" card. Toggle "Duplicate detection" on and set the similarity threshold (0–1; higher = stricter, fewer matches). When enabled, the create-item page shows a pre-create panel listing potential duplicates with similarity scores before the save — the user can open a match or proceed with the create.

API

POST /api/ai/check-duplicates
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "collection": "companies",
  "data": { "name": "ACME Corporation Inc.", "city": "Berlin" }
}

→ {
  "data": {
    "matches": [
      { "id": "uuid", "similarity": 0.93, "preview": { "name": "Acme Corp.", "city": "Berlin" } }
    ]
  }
}
Detection is advisory — it never blocks the create. The toggle and threshold live in nivaro_ai_collection_settings alongside the validation rules. Embeddings use the same provider chain as semantic search.

AI design helpers

Four admin-only helpers that propose configuration and never write it on their own: a layout review, field help text drafts, a role designed from a sentence, and saved views suggested per role. Each suggestion is applied one at a time by an admin, is logged, and can be undone.

Layout review

Layout editor → settings rail → **Review this layout**. Rule checks run first and are counted, never guessed: a step with more than 15 fields or a section with more than 12, a required field inside a section that starts collapsed, a required field the layout hides, required or rule-bound fields with no help text, two fields with the same label, and empty sections. When AI is set up, the model adds unclear labels (with a better one) and help text for the fields that need it. Every field it names must be on the layout; anything else is dropped.

Each finding names the field and, where it can, carries a fix: **Open section**, **Move field** (to the emptiest sibling step or section), **Add help text**, **Rename** or **Show field**. Help text and labels are editable before you apply them and are written as this layout's overrides, so other layouts keep theirs. A layout version is captured before every fix, so the newest fix offers **Undo** and any of them can be rolled back from Version history.

A crowded step or section also offers a whole restructure: **Split into 3 steps…** (or sections) previews every change as a list — the new steps, where each sits and which fields move into it — and **Apply all** makes them as one change through the editor, so a single Undo in the top bar reverses the whole split. When AI is set up the model groups related fields and names the parts; its answer is used only if it places every field exactly once, otherwise the fields are split into equal runs in their current order ("Details (2)", "Details (3)"). Hidden fields stay where they are. The single **Move field** fix stays available beside it.

Field help text drafts

Collection → Settings → **Field help text** lists the visible fields with no help text. **Draft help text** asks the AI for one or two sentences per field, built from its type, choices, validation rules, field rules, cascade parents, relation and formula, plus the collection note and the data guide (Settings → AI Features). Accept, edit or skip each draft. Accepting writes the field's help text; the activity entry (ai-help-text) keeps the previous text.

Design a role from a description

Roles → **Design with AI**. Describe the role ("Reads invoices in Zone 3, approves inventory requests, cannot export") and the AI proposes a name, policies with field limits and row filters, pages to switch off, and User Scopes for its members. Every collection, field, row-filter column, page and scope value is checked against this instance; a grant whose field limit or row filter cannot be kept is dropped whole rather than widened, and each drop is listed. The designer never proposes admin access.

Edit the change set (remove grants, field limits or page restrictions, rename), then **Run simulator on the edits**: the simulator shows each collection's create/read/update/delete outcome and how many rows a member would see under the read filter. **Create role** is only possible while the simulation matches the proposal — the server checks the simulation's fingerprint. User Scopes belong to people, so creating the role does not apply them: they come back as scopes_to_set_per_member for you to set on each member after adding them.

Suggested views per role

Roles → a role → **Suggested views** → **Find suggestions**. The API log of the last 14 days shows which filters people applied by hand in collection lists. A filter set counts when two or more members of the role applied it, or one member applied it on three separate days (shown only for roles with three or more members, so one person's filtering is not singled out). Filter sets a shared view visible to that role already holds are left out, as are admin roles. Each suggestion shows the filters, the most used sort, and how many members applied it; the AI names it from field names and operators only (the values people filtered by never leave the instance) and picks columns from the collection's real fields. **Create view** writes a shared saved view scoped to the role.

API

POST /api/ai-design/layouts/:id/review        { ai?: boolean }  → { findings[], ai_used, ai_error, ai_configured }
POST /api/ai-design/layouts/:id/apply         { fix }           → { applied, undo_version_id }
POST /api/ai-design/layouts/:id/command       { text }          → { intents[], explanation, dropped } (422 when it cannot)
GET  /api/ai-design/help-text/:collection                       → { candidates[] }
POST /api/ai-design/help-text/:collection/draft { fields? }     → { drafts[] }
POST /api/ai-design/help-text/:collection/apply { field, text } → { field, note, previous }
POST /api/ai-design/roles/design   { description, ui_routes? }  → { proposal, dropped[], simulation[], hash }
POST /api/ai-design/roles/simulate { proposal, ui_routes? }     → { proposal, dropped[], simulation[], hash }
POST /api/ai-design/roles/apply    { proposal, hash }           → 201 { id, name, policies, scopes_to_set_per_member }
POST /api/ai-design/role-views/suggest { days?, ai? }           → { suggestions[], ai_used, ai_error }
POST /api/ai-design/role-views/apply { role, collection, name, filters, sort?, columns? } → 201 { id }

Crowded-group findings carry change_set { kind: 'split', title, steps[], ops[], base_rev, parts, source };
the editor applies ops through its draft (POST /api/collection-layouts/:id/ops), one batch.
All routes require an administrator. Drafting, role design and commands answer 503 when AI is not set up;
the layout review and view suggestions still run their rule checks without it.

Connect an AI assistant (MCP)

Nivaro speaks the Model Context Protocol, so ChatGPT, Claude (claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code), Codex and Cursor can read and work with your data in a conversation: look up records and their history, run your custom queries, check My Work and queues, comment, create tasks and move records through their pipeline. The assistant always acts as **you** — your role, row rules and User Scopes apply exactly as in the app, and everything it changes is recorded as your change.

There are two ways in. The **hosted endpoint** https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp needs nothing installed: the assistant signs you in through Nivaro (OAuth) or sends an API key. The **npm server** @nivaro/mcp runs on your own machine over stdio with an API key — useful for desktop tools when you prefer a key to a sign-in.

ChatGPT and claude.ai connect from their own cloud, so they can only reach a Nivaro that is reachable from the internet. An instance on a private network works with the tools that run on your machine — Claude Code, Claude Desktop (npm server), Codex and Cursor — while you are on that network.

ChatGPT

  • Settings → Apps & Connectors → Advanced settings → turn on **Developer mode** (your workspace admin may need to allow it).
  • Create a connector: name it Nivaro, set the MCP server URL to https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp, authentication **OAuth**.
  • ChatGPT opens Nivaro’s sign-in, then a consent page naming ChatGPT. **Allow** connects it. ChatGPT asks before running tools that change data — Nivaro marks every tool as read-only or not, and deletes as destructive.

Claude (claude.ai and Claude Desktop)

  • Settings → Connectors → **Add custom connector** → URL https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp. Claude signs you in through Nivaro the same way.
  • Claude Desktop on a private network: use the npm server instead — add it to claude_desktop_config.json (see below) with an API key.

Claude Code

# sign in through Nivaro (run /mcp in Claude Code to finish the sign-in)
claude mcp add --transport http nivaro https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp

# or with an API key
claude mcp add --transport http nivaro https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer nvk_your_key"

Codex

# sign in through Nivaro
codex mcp add nivaro --url https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp
codex mcp login nivaro

# or ~/.codex/config.toml with an API key in the environment
[mcp_servers.nivaro]
url = "https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp"
bearer_token_env_var = "NIVARO_TOKEN"

The npm server (stdio)

For any client that launches local servers (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex, Claude Code). It needs NIVARO_URL (the API origin, no /api) and NIVARO_TOKEN (an nvk_ API key from API Keys, or a static token).

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nivaro": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@nivaro/mcp"],
      "env": { "NIVARO_URL": "https://<your-nivaro>", "NIVARO_TOKEN": "nvk_your_key" }
    }
  }
}

What an assistant can do

  • Learn the data model (collections, fields, relations) and read, filter and total records.
  • Create, update and delete records — creates rehearse first unless told to store, deletes need an explicit confirm — and move records through their pipeline.
  • Work with My Work, queues, comments and mentions, tasks, revision history, custom queries, notifications, files (details only, never contents) and search.
  • Ask Nivaro’s own data assistant (Ask AI) a question.
  • Work the support desk: list and read support requests, claim one, reply and change its status. You see your own requests; desk members and administrators see the desk, exactly as in Support. Claim, reply and status changes rehearse first unless told to go ahead.
  • See the approval steps waiting on you and approve or reject one with a note. The approval chain rules apply as in the app, and a decision rehearses first unless told to go ahead.
  • Look up the SLA clock and the at-risk reasons for one record or a list of records. Records you cannot open are left out.
  • Administrators can also ask why a person cannot see a record (explain_access): which gate hid it, with reasons only and no record values.
  • Read dashboards and reports: list_dashboards lists the dashboards and Report Studio reports you can open, read_dashboard gives a dashboard’s widget figures and run_report a report’s. Every figure is computed as you, the same way the widget computes it for you in the app — a widget you cannot see says so instead of showing a number. The saved filter bar and date range apply unless the assistant asks for others.
  • Chat, only when you allowed it: list_chat_rooms, read_chat_messages and post_chat_message reach only the rooms you can open. Posting rehearses first unless told to post, goes out as you, and every message shows **via app ·** and the app’s name beside it.
  • Administrators also get read-only operations tools: health and readiness, runtime and database pool, Traffic Map summary, scheduled jobs and their runs, and a CPU profile of the API. Nothing restarts, pauses or reconfigures anything.
  • Administrators also get layout tools: describe_layout (a form in plain terms, or every form of a collection), which_form (which form a record gets for a role, and why), explain_field (why a field shows, hides or is read-only for a role on a record) and propose_layout_ops. A proposal never changes a form: it waits under Proposals in the layout editor until an administrator tries it on the canvas and keeps it, or rejects it.

This instance’s own tools

Beyond the built-in set, an instance can offer tools of its own, managed on **Developer → MCP → Assistant tools** (/mcp/tools). An administrator can expose a saved query or a flow as a named tool: the query’s parameters (or the inputs you list, for a flow) become the tool’s input, and it runs as the person calling — the query’s own access level and user scopes decide what comes back, and a flow runs with the caller as the person who triggered it. Choose who may call it (administrators, or everyone signed in) and whether it only reads. An API key limited to named collections never gets flow tools (a flow runs as the person and would reach past the key’s collections), and an administrator on such a key is not treated as an administrator here. Extensions add tools with ctx.mcp.registerTool; they are listed on the same page.

The hosted endpoint lists each of these tools by name. The npm server reaches the same tools through list_instance_tools and call_instance_tool. Both call GET /api/mcp-tools and POST /api/mcp-tools/:name/call as the key’s user; named tools are stored in nivaro_settings.mcp_tools (migration 473).

Sign-in or API key

Signing in (OAuth) connects the assistant as you, with your permissions, and needs nothing stored on your machine; access tokens last an hour and renew themselves for 30 days of use. An API key gives you finer control: a key with **narrowed scopes** is held to them, a key with **row restrictions** sees only those rows, and a **sandbox** key can explore everything and never changes anything — a safe way to try an assistant out.

Chat needs its own permission

Chat is never part of a connection by default. When you sign in, the consent page has a box **Also let it read and post in your chat conversations** — ticked only if the app asked for chat, and yours to untick. Without it the connection gets no chat tools, is refused on every chat route, and sees chat notifications only as "a chat message", never their words. Connecting again with a different choice changes the existing connection at once. For an API key, an administrator sets **Chat for AI assistants** on the key (Off, Read, or Read and post); * scopes never include chat. Every chat message posted with an API key or a connected app — through MCP or not — shows **via app ·** and the key’s or app’s name (cleaned, at most 60 characters; a connected app chose its own name, so it is always shown as app text, never as a person), and its Activity entry names the OAuth client id or API key id.

Connected apps

Every assistant you allowed is a connection: GET /api/oauth/connections lists them (name, when you connected, when it was last used, and whether it may use chat) and DELETE /api/oauth/connections/:id disconnects one — its tokens stop working at once. Connecting and disconnecting are logged in Activity (oauth-connect, oauth-revoke). Suspending an account ends its connections too: every request checks the account is still active.

Live record updates

Connect to /api/mcp?live=1 instead of /api/mcp and the assistant can follow records. Every record is a resource, nivaro://record/<collection>/<id>; reading it reads the record as you. Subscribing to one tells the assistant when it changes: Nivaro sends notifications/resources/updated with the record’s address and the names of the fields that changed (_meta), never their values. The assistant reads the record again to see the new values, with your permissions.

  • A live connection gets a session id on its first answer and listens on GET /api/mcp (an event stream). DELETE /api/mcp ends the session.
  • You can only follow a record you can read, at most 50 at a time per connection. Access is checked again every two minutes: a record you can no longer read is dropped, with one last notice.
  • Sessions last 24 hours after the last use. The event stream closes when your sign-in ends; the assistant reconnects with its renewed sign-in and keeps its subscriptions.
  • A plain /api/mcp connection works exactly as before, with no session.

MCP console

Developer → MCP → Console (/mcp/console, administrators) lists the tools an assistant connected as you would get, with a form built from each tool’s inputs (or JSON, for the raw arguments). Running a tool goes through the same MCP server the endpoint uses, as you, and shows the result as the assistant sees it, the raw JSON answer, how long it took, how large it is, and every API call the tool made.

Tools that change data start in **dry run**. A tool that can rehearse (create_item) rehearses: rules and validation run and nothing is stored. Any other tool runs but its changes are held: the console does not send them and lists each one under API calls. Turn dry run off and confirm to run it for real.

Your profile has a **What my agents did** tab (/profile?tab=agents). It lists each connected app with its last 14 days of tool calls (calls a day, refused and failed calls, the tools it used most, how much it read back) and a Disconnect button, then every tool call newest first: the app, the tool, the record it touched and how it ended. Open a call to see the changes it made. Each change can be undone while nothing else has changed the record since: an edit puts back the values from before, a new record is deleted. Undo runs as you, so your permissions and the record’s rules apply, and it is logged (mcp-undo).

For administrators

  • **MCP → Connections** (/mcp) lists every assistant connected to this instance across people, with the same 14-day figures, and lets you disconnect a sign-in or switch off a key.
  • Each connection may make a set number of tool calls a minute (default 120; 0 means no limit), and you can give one connection its own limit. Over the limit the assistant gets HTTP 429 with Retry-After and a message saying why, so it can tell its person and wait.
  • Idle review: a signed-in connection unused for 60 days is pointed out to its owner, the owner is warned seven days before 90 days, and at 90 days it is disconnected (job mcp-idle-review, daily on deployed instances). Both day counts are settings at the top of the page; the Idle tab shows what the next run will do.
  • On the Traffic Map each app is its own caller, named MCP: <app> — the name the app registered with, or the API key’s name — grouped under AI assistants.
  • Every request made through /api/mcp is marked in the request log with its connection and tool, which is where all of these figures come from; the log keeps 14 days.

Settings and how it works

  • MCP_HTTP=off turns the hosted endpoint off (the npm server keeps working with a key); MCP_OAUTH=off turns sign-in off and leaves API keys working on /api/mcp.
  • MCP_SESSIONS=off turns live sessions off: ?live=1 is ignored and every connection is answered without a session.
  • MCP_PUBLIC_URL names the address assistants reach this API on, when it is not the API’s own host — the sign-in must start and end there, and that address must be registered with your identity provider.
  • Discovery: /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource and /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server. Clients register themselves (/oauth/register, public clients only), must use PKCE (S256), and may only return to https addresses or to localhost on your machine.
  • The npm server asks GET /api/mcp/capabilities at startup which optional tools the key gets (admin_tools, chat: none, read or post).
  • Each /api/mcp request is answered on its own (a live session only remembers its subscriptions, in Redis), so any API replica can serve it, and every tool call inside it is an ordinary API request — rate limits, the maintenance freeze and the request log apply to each call.

Microsoft Integration

Nivaro ships with built-in Microsoft 365 integrations. Configure them in Settings.

Teams notifications

Set teams_webhook_url in Settings to an incoming Teams webhook URL. When a user is mentioned in a comment, a Teams MessageCard is automatically posted to that webhook.

Azure AD group → role mapping

Set ad_group_role_map in Settings to a JSON object mapping AD group names to Nivaro role IDs. On OIDC login, the server resolves the user's AD groups and auto-assigns the first matching role.

// ad_group_role_map example (JSON stored in Settings):
{
  "Admins":   "admin-role-uuid",
  "Finance":  "finance-role-uuid",
  "ReadOnly": "viewer-role-uuid"
}

OIDC authentication

All auth flows through Microsoft OIDC (PKCE). First name, last name, and email are synced from the OIDC token on every login. No separate user creation required.

Directory lookups (User.Read.All)

Login enrichment only refreshes a profile when that person signs in. With User.Read.All granted to the app registration as an **application** permission (admin-consented), the server reads any tenant user with its own token: GET /api/directory/users?q= searches by name or email, GET /api/directory/users/:key returns one entry (Graph id, UPN or email) with their manager and the Nivaro account it maps to, and POST /api/directory/sync/:userId (admin) pulls a directory entry onto a Nivaro profile — the directory wins for every field it has a value for; blanks never clear a stored value. GET /api/directory/status reports whether the app token actually carries the permission, and the Users page shows the same verdict: the Microsoft directory card on a user, and a "Find in Microsoft directory" search inside Add User that fills the form from the tenant.

A delegated User.Read.All is not enough: it only widens the token of the person logging in. The app token must carry the role — the status endpoint says "no Graph roles" until admin consent is granted. Credentials default to the OIDC app registration; GRAPH_TENANT_ID / GRAPH_CLIENT_ID / GRAPH_CLIENT_SECRET override them when a separate app owns the directory permission.

Directory sync — is this person still with the company?

Every user carries a directory verdict: **With the company** (found, account enabled), **Disabled in Azure**, **Not in directory**, or not checked yet. Three ways to take it: the nightly directory-sync job (04:15; Settings → Microsoft → Directory sync switches it on, and it skips itself until the app token carries User.Read.All), the **Check directory** button on the Users page (POST /api/directory/check, everyone or a selected list), and the per-user check — the refresh glyph beside each verdict pill, or **Sync from directory** on the user page (POST /api/directory/sync/:id, which also pulls the profile). Every check — nightly, bulk or single — also refreshes the profile fields, the manager and the photo of each person the directory has (send pull_profile: false to skip that). A check asks the directory only about the people in the user table, 15 per call by stored directory id, then mail, then UPN, with photos fetched 20 per call; the tenant itself is never walked.

Someone the directory no longer has — missing or disabled — is **suspended** while the "Suspend people the directory no longer has" switch is on (the default). A suspension is never lifted by the check, and redaction stays a separate, deliberate action. The Users page filter **Directory: Departed** lists them, and **Hand off N departed** moves everything they still hold (queue claims, open record ownerships, tasks, owner-group seats, delegate chains, subscriptions) to one successor in a single pass — the same offboarding run each user page offers alone. Admins get one notification per nightly run naming who left; GET /api/directory/report carries the last run and the current counts.

SLA Tracking

SLA Rules define time limits for how long a workflow instance can remain in a given state. The system tracks warning thresholds (% of duration elapsed) and full breaches, with optional escalation user notifications.

Creating an SLA rule

Navigate to Workflow → Deadlines & risk → SLA rules. Click New Rule:

FieldDescription
NameDisplay label for the rule.
Workflow TemplateThe workflow this rule applies to.
State KeyThe specific workflow state to measure time in.
Duration (hours)Total allowed time in this state.
Warning Threshold %Notification fires when this % of duration has elapsed. Default 80%.
Business Hours OnlyWhen enabled, only counts working hours towards elapsed time — the days, hours and holidays from Settings → SLA, evaluated in the SLA timezone (or the record's regional clock when its region is mapped).
Notify on WarningSend in-app notification to escalation user at warning threshold.
Notify on BreachSend in-app notification to escalation user on full breach.
Escalation UserOptional. User to notify on warning/breach.

Checking SLA status

The SlaBadge component can be embedded on any item page. It queries GET /api/sla/status/:collection/:item and renders a colored badge:

BadgeMeaning
On Track (green)Below warning threshold.
Warning (amber)Past warning threshold but not yet breached.
Breached (red)Over the full allowed duration.
No SLA (gray)No active SLA rule for the current workflow state.
SLA elapsed time is computed on-demand from workflow history timestamps — no background job required. Business hours use the schedule and timezone configured in Settings → SLA (default Mon–Fri, 09:00–17:00) — the zone matters: an empty timezone means the API server's clock, which is UTC in a deployed container. Regional clocks can override the zone per record.

Queue SLA Timers

The collection browser shows a live SLA column for workflow-bound collections that have active SLA rules — turning any filtered list into a work queue with countdown timers. No configuration beyond existing SLA rules is needed.

What you see

BadgeMeaning
Green — "Xh left"Within the SLA duration and below the warning threshold.
