Saving takes two clicks and writes an activity row. The environment variables below are the defaults the card starts from.

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
TRAFFIC_SAMPLE_ABOVE_RPS300Requests per second above which the ticker shows 1 event in N. 0 never samples. The Map data card on the map overrides it.
TRAFFIC_N_PLUS_ONE_TRIPS40Average round trips per request before an entity gets the N+1 badge.
TRAFFIC_FANOUT_LIMIT60Calls in one page load before a screen is flagged for fan-out.
TRAFFIC_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS60000The proxy read timeout the near-timeout detector judges whole requests against.
TRAFFIC_CAPACITY_RPSunsetA fixed request-per-second ceiling for the headroom gauge. Unset = the best sustained minute from the request log.
TRACE_SLOW_MS1000Requests slower than this are kept for the Slow requests panel.

GET|PUT /api/traffic-map/node-info                 → what a node is (and an admin's own text)
GET  /api/traffic-map/environment                  → the band: name and tier
GET  /api/traffic-map/overhead                     → the map's own cost
GET  /api/traffic-map/compare/windows?…            → two windows from the request log
GET|POST|DELETE /api/traffic-map/breakers          → circuit breakers
GET  /api/traffic-map/history/timelapse?range=24h|7d → playback frames, people, markers
GET  /api/traffic-map/history/search?kind=…        → last hit, first error, busiest hour
GET  /api/traffic-map/history/route-latency?key=&route=&hours= → duration histogram
GET  /api/traffic-map/history/slow-params?key=&route=&hours=   → parameters of slow requests

GET  /api/traffic-map/capacity/what-if?traffic_pct=&add_replicas=&job=&to_minute=

socket  admin:join {room: 'traffic-map'}           → one 'traffic-map:frame' per API process per second while watched
socket  admin:join {room: 'traffic-map', frames: 'batch'} → one 'traffic-map:batch' per second: every process's frames, unchanged fields left out (same / ext_same); emit 'traffic-map:resync' for a full one

Live Updates

Open lists, records, queues and chat update as other people work, over one Socket.io connection per browser (the leader tab carries the collection feed for every tab). The Realtime console (Operations → Realtime) shows who is connected, how, and what it costs.

When websockets are blocked

Every client tries the websocket first. When a proxy strips the upgrade, the same connect attempt falls through to HTTP long-polling; when the server refuses polling too, the leader tab reads collection changes from the read-only GET /api/events/stream (SSE) and relays them to the other tabs. Chat, presence and watch rooms wait for a socket.

  • Long-polling needs **sticky sessions** behind a load balancer: every poll must reach the process holding that connection. Where the balancer is not sticky, set SOCKET_POLLING=off and blocked clients use the SSE stream instead.
  • The Sockets tab shows each socket's transport (websocket or polling) and counts the SSE fallback streams apart.
  • The SDK realtime client and every admin socket use the same order: websocket, then polling.

Compression and payload size

Frames over 1 KB are compressed (per-message deflate; SOCKET_COMPRESSION=off turns it off — it costs CPU per socket). The **Payload size** tab counts messages and bytes written to sockets on this API process, by event type and by room kind (every record room of a collection is one row), heaviest first, so a heavy broadcast can be found and trimmed. Bytes are counted before compression; a broadcast counts once per socket that received it. **Reset counters** starts over, to see the effect of a change.

Bursts are merged

An import or bulk action writing thousands of rows used to send thousands of collection:update messages to every watching tab. The server now coalesces per socket: the first change to a collection goes out at once, and the rest of each one-second window collapse into ONE message listing the ids (coalesced: true, items: [...], or many: true past 200 ids), so each tab refreshes once. Only clients that say they understand it (features: ['coalesce'] in client:hello) receive merged messages; others keep one message per change. Shared components read them through updateItemIds() / updateTouches().

Sockets close when the sign-in ends

A socket is bound to what signed it in: the session, a View-as (masquerade) token, a static token or a named API key — never to the account alone. Logout, a revoked session (Security → Sessions, "sign out everywhere else"), a session past the session policy, an ended View-as, a rotated token, a switched-off or expired API key and a suspended account all close that sign-in's sockets on every API process (through the Redis adapter, and a 30-second sweep on each process catches anything nothing announced). The tab is told why (session:ended) and returns to sign-in — unless the browser already holds a newer sign-in, in which case it simply reconnects. The SSE stream ends the same way at its next heartbeat. A socket or stream opened through an API key carries that key's scopes and row restrictions. A View-as tab never falls back to the SSE stream (it could only open on the administrator's own cookie).

Room access follows permission changes

Rooms used to be checked only when joined. Now a change to a person (role, status, user scopes, offboarding) or to access everywhere (roles and policies, teams, scope dimensions, channel membership, tree permissions) re-checks the rooms their open sockets hold — collections by read permission, records by the same row filter and scope gate as GET /items, chat rooms by the chat visibility rule, watch and presence rooms by admin access — and leaves the ones that no longer pass. The client hears access:changed { rooms_left } (room names only) and re-reads what is on screen.

Reconnect banner and stale marks

When the connection drops for more than a few seconds, a strip says "Live updates paused, reconnecting" and collection lists and queue worklists show a **May be stale** mark. After the reconnect and the missed-event catch-up the strip says live updates resumed, and when the gap was too long to replay it says the page's lists and records were reloaded. Hosts give shared components this state through the optional status() / onStatus() on their RealtimeAdapter; RealtimeStatusBanner and RealtimeStaleMark render it.

Server time

When the socket signs in, the client times three time:sync round trips and takes its clock offset from the fastest one. Relative labels ("2m ago"), due-in countdowns and retry times then use serverNow(), so two machines with drifting clocks agree. Offsets under a second are ignored.

Verifying live updates

Realtime → Verification holds four tools that prove live updates work rather than assume it. All are for administrators.

  • **Delivery service level.** How long events take to reach the browser, against a target (default: 95% within 2 seconds, set beside the other service levels on the Health page as delivery_good_pct / delivery_p95_ms in slo_targets). Two sources feed it: the delivery probe the Realtime delivery monitor runs every 5 minutes (a probe that never arrives counts as a miss), and real tabs, which answer one event in 50 with the time it reached them on the server clock (REALTIME_ACK_EVERY, 0 = off) — plus each server's first event after 30 seconds without one (REALTIME_ACK_FLOOR_S, 0 = off), so a read-heavy day is still measured. With a realtime tier the web process stamps the event and the realtime process holding the tab takes the answer; a server with SOCKETS=off skips the probe (it has no sockets to probe) rather than record a miss. An answer counts only from a signed-in connection, only when it echoes the exact send stamp the server kept for that event, and at most a couple every 10 seconds per person. Not kept in cloud mode. Figures are per server; the burn rates use the same multi-window rule as the request service levels, and a burn of 14× in the last hour or 6× over 6 hours raises an issue. For your own alert rules, a metric definition with source {"type":"realtime_slo","metric":"burn_1h"} (or burn_6h, p95_ms, good_pct, samples) is evaluated after every monitor run. The readiness check **The live-update delivery check hears from clients** warns, and the Delivery by node monitor fails, when connected tabs received sampled events in the last 15 minutes and not one answered — the figures would otherwise sit unchanged and look healthy. GET /api/realtime/delivery-slo carries the same reading as acks.
  • **Connection drills.** Delay every event, drop a share of them, or cut the connection once or repeatedly, for one person, everyone in a room or a share of everyone, for 5 to 600 seconds. The drill reaches every server; the table shows how many connections it touched, how many people came back after a cut and how their catch-up answered (replayed or reloaded). Refused in cloud mode, and on a production server unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true.
  • **Leak audit.** Checks a sample of the events sent to each connection, after they are sent, against what that person could open themselves: the collection, each record (row rules and user scopes) and each field name. A miss is logged with the event and room and raised as one issue per event, collection and kind; nothing is held back. Start a timed audit from the tab, or keep one on with REALTIME_LEAK_AUDIT_RATE (a share between 0 and 1). At most 20 checks a second per server. Never runs in cloud mode.
  • **Replay on staging.** Download a capture of the last 5 to 15 minutes of record events (ids only) with the room mix and connection counts, then run pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run realtime:replay -- --capture <file> --target <staging> --token <admin token> --speed 1|2|5. Simulated connections join copies of the captured rooms (rtreplay:<run>:<room>, so nobody on staging receives a replayed event), the target sends the captured events through its normal path, and the report gives delivery p50 / p95 / p99, loss, API CPU, event-loop delay and Redis load. The script refuses the capture's own server, production environments from the Environments registry, this checkout's hosts and TRAFFIC_REPLAY_SHARED_HOSTS; the target refuses unless it runs with REALTIME_REPLAY=on.

Per tenant (cloud)

In cloud mode sockets, events and bytes are also kept per tenant. A tenant's Realtime console shows only its own event and room figures; the operator reads every tenant, noisiest first (bytes and events in the last whole minute, then open sockets), from GET /admin/realtime-tenants with the provisioning secret — per API process, like /admin/traffic-tenants.

One process serves several tenants, so every live feed stays inside its tenant: record, item, chat, pulse, presence and watch rooms are named t:<tenant>:<room> (self-hosted names are unchanged; presence sessions are kept per tenant too), an SSE stream delivers only writes made in the tenant it was opened under, and GraphQL subscriptions (itemMutated, workflowStateChanged, pipelineStateChanged) listen on per-tenant topics — the tenant rides each event across replicas. A graphql-ws connection resolves its tenant from its host like a socket does and signs in against that tenant's database; one with no tenant hears nothing. Workflow and pipeline state subscriptions need read access to the record, and each subscriber receives the instance as they would read it (events carry ids only). A socket may only watch a real collection: collection:join refuses names such as orders:5.

Command Center

The Command Center at /command is a live operations wallboard: a map of your records and people, a pipeline flow board, a risk strip, throughput numbers, and a ticker of recent activity — all on one dark, glanceable screen. Everything refreshes on its own (the snapshot every 20 seconds, the map every 60), and a Refresh button in the header re-pulls the whole board on demand.

The page works for every authenticated user — each pane only shows what that person is allowed to read. Only the System health rail is admin-only.

The live map

The map is an OpenStreetMap view with two kinds of layer, toggled by the chips in the panel header. Record layers show one pin per record of a geocoded collection (locations by default); the People chip shows green bubbles for who is online and where. Clicking a chip that is already selected hides that layer; clicking a different collection chip switches to it.

  • Record pins come from any collection that has latitude/longitude columns (latitude/lat and longitude/lng/lon are auto-detected), read through the normal items API — so role permissions, row-level security, and user scopes all apply to what you see. The first 500 records are plotted.
  • Pin color follows the record: red with a pulsing ring when its SLA is breached, amber on SLA warning, otherwise the workflow state color. Nearby pins cluster into a numbered disc — click a cluster to zoom in, click a single pin to open the record.
  • People bubbles appear at geocoded office locations (one bubble per office, sized by how many people are online there) and, for people without a resolved office, at region centroids computed from the average position of that region’s locations. A region needs at least two geocoded locations before it earns a centroid.
  • The status line under the map reports how many records are plotted, whether the 500-record cap was hit, and how many people groups are on.

Flow board, people, and ticker

  • Pipeline flow — one bar per workflow-bound collection you can read, segmented by state: each segment’s width is that state’s share of the open records, tinted with the state color, with a legend of counts underneath. Clicking a segment opens that collection’s browser.
  • People on now — everyone currently online (active in the last 70 seconds), grouped by office first and then by region, with each person’s name as a pill. Clicking a group flies the map to that office or region. Non-admins with restricted user scopes see only colleagues whose scopes overlap their own on every restricted dimension.
  • Header strip — live clock, online/idle counts, transitions today with a delta versus the same time yesterday (from workflow history), and a red open-issues pill that links to /issues when anything is open.
  • Risk numbers — at-risk and tracked counts come from the materialized queue caches, and open issues from the issue log seen in the last 90 days.
  • Live ticker — the most recent creates, updates, deletes, and pipeline transitions across business collections, filtered to collections you can read. Each pill shows who did what and links to the record. A quiet ticker for a low-permission user is normal.

System health rail (admins)

Admins get an extra rail: database and Redis status dots, error and request counts for the last hour, running and recently failed background jobs, process memory, and event-loop lag. The server never sends this block to non-admins, so the panel simply does not exist for them.

Where office locations come from

On instances using Microsoft sign-in, each login also captures the user’s organizational profile from Microsoft Graph under the standard User.Read scope — no extra admin consent is needed. Alongside the existing title, company, department, and phone, Nivaro now captures office location, city, state, country, employee ID, and preferred language, and stores them on the user record.

  • The directory (Microsoft Entra / Azure AD) is the source of truth: every login re-writes these fields from Graph, so a value edited by hand is overwritten at the person’s next sign-in. A field Graph does not return keeps its previous value rather than being cleared.
  • The Graph call runs inside the login with a 5-second budget and fails quietly — a slow or unavailable Graph never blocks anyone from signing in; the profile just stays as it was.
  • When a login carries an office location, it is geocoded in the background: first against your own locations collection (an exact street-address match wins and costs nothing), then via OpenStreetMap’s public geocoder. The resolved coordinates become that person’s office pin on the Command Center map.
  • Geocoding remembers which address it resolved, so an unchanged office costs nothing on later logins; only a changed address triggers a new lookup. An address that cannot be resolved is retried at the next login, and that person appears in region bubbles (or a "No location set" group) instead.
Office location is visible to everyone in the people directory, like title and department. Employee ID and city stay admin-only.

Wallboard & Pulse

Wallboard (TV mode)

/wallboard renders a chrome-free, dark, full-screen queue dashboard for ops-floor displays: giant stat tiles (total, unowned, SLA warning/breached, at risk) and a by-state distribution, auto-rotating across your queues every 20 seconds and refreshing every minute.

Pulse (live activity stream)

/activity/live streams every activity entry the moment it happens over an admin-only Socket.io room, with a per-minute sparkline. Use it to watch a migration, an import, or a busy Monday in real time.

Both are read-only surfaces over existing data — no new tables, no configuration.

Relationship Explorer

Every record form has a Relationships button in its header. It opens a map of the records linked to this one, grouped by the link: what the record points at (vendor, project, creator), what points at it (lines, forecasts, notes), and records joined through a many-to-many link. Expand any record to see what it connects to in turn; click a record to open it.

GET /api/record-graph/:collection/:id
→ { "data": { "node": {collection, id, label, collection_label},
              "groups": [{ "direction": "out|in|m2m", "field", "label", "collection",
                           "collection_label", "total", "items": [{collection, id, label}] }],
              "edges": 29, "truncated": false } }
  • Every record in the answer is read as the viewer (roles, row filters, User Scopes): a group the viewer cannot read is left out and counts are what the viewer can see. A record outside their access answers 404.
  • Up to 12 records per group; total says how many there are. Polymorphic links are split per target collection.
  • A relation row naming a table that no longer exists drops that group rather than failing the map.
  • Shared components RecordGraphSheet / RecordGraphExplorer (exported from @nivaro/react), so headless hosts get the same explorer.

Built-in Bug Reporter

The floating bug button (bottom-right on every admin page) files reports straight into the issue log: your description and severity, an automatic screenshot of the page, the last console errors/warnings, and your route + browser details.

Screenshots are downscaled JPEGs capped at 2MB, stored on the issue and shown in the expanded issue detail. The list view never carries the blob.

Journey Trail

A session-by-session breadcrumb of every admin page a user visited, with time spent on each — session-replay insight without recording anything on screen. Built from the same presence pings that power the live map, persisted with 30-day retention.

GET /api/journeys/user/:id?date=YYYY-MM-DD&app=   # sessions + steps for one day
GET /api/journeys/days/:id?app=                     # which of the last 30 days have data, + apps seen
  • Admin-only — this is user tracking; the API refuses non-admins.
  • Durations stamp when the user moves to the next page or disconnects (capped at 8h against dangling sessions).
  • UI: the Journey Trail card on a user profile (admin view), with a day picker of active days.
  • Rows purge automatically after 30 days in the daily retention pass.
  • Portals too: a front end built on @nivaro/react calls usePageAt({ app: 'efp', path }) inside its realtime provider and its pages land in the same trail, labelled with the app. ?app= narrows either route to one front end ('admin' includes rows from before the label existed); the card shows an app filter and a per-session app chip once a person has used more than one. Portal pages are listed, not linked.

Session Replay

Full rrweb screen recording of admin sessions: watch exactly what a user saw and did, scrubbed like video. Off by default — flip the switch on the Session Replays page and every admin session starts recording.

  • Privacy: every input and every record field value is masked client-side before events leave the browser (see Masking rules below); add the nvr-no-record class to block any element entirely.
  • Events batch every 10 seconds; a full DOM snapshot every 60 seconds keeps replays seekable.
  • Recordings cap at 15MB (then mark truncated) and purge after the retention period (7 days unless changed on the Session Replays page); after 3 days they move from the database to file storage.
  • Watching, listing and deleting are admin-only; a recording can only be appended to by its own user.
  • Tell your team before enabling — this records their screens.

Uploads that survive bad networks

A chunk that cannot be sent — the browser is offline, the request fails or the server answers 5xx — waits in the browser (IndexedDB, at most about 20MB per tab, oldest dropped first) and is retried with backoff from 2 seconds up to a minute, and as soon as the browser comes back online. Reloading the tab within 10 minutes continues the same recording instead of starting a new one, and whatever the previous page had not sent goes first. When a page is closed or reloaded, the last few seconds are sent with the request that outlives the page (fetch keepalive); anything that does not fit goes on the next load. A recording that is closed or has reached its size cap still stops for good, and the next page load starts a new one. The headless hook in @nivaro/react does the same.

Realtime events in a replay

A recording also notes the realtime events the page received: the event name, the room, up to ten record ids and up to twenty field names, never a value. Reconnects, missed-event catch-up and full reloads after a long gap show too. In the player they are the Live tab beside Console and Network, and a connection change is a violet tick on the scrubber, so a screen that changed by itself points at the event that did it. The track has its own limit of 800 entries per page load, after which one note says the log is full. Only the first tab of a browser (the one holding the live connection) records these.

Masking rules

Besides every input, the recorders mask the value of every field on a record — in the edit form and the read view — so a replay shows the layout and what the person did, not the data. Settings → Session replay → Masking lists fields that are safe to watch (a status, a code) as collection.field, or *.field for any collection; those show in replays and everything else stays masked. Field labels always show.

  • Mask rich text (on by default): editors such as notes and descriptions show as asterisks wherever they appear, even in an allowed field.
  • Mask file names (on by default): file names are masked and file thumbnails blocked, in file fields and the file library, even in an allowed field.
  • Passwords are never shown. Text in attributes (a tooltip, an image’s alt text) is not masked; keep sensitive values out of them or mark the element nvr-no-record.
  • The rules apply to the admin app and to frontends using useSessionRecorder from @nivaro/react; a changed rule reaches a recorder on its next page load. Recordings already made are not changed.

Recording cost

Every uploaded chunk names the page (route pattern) it was recorded on and the frontend build that recorded it. DB Health → Session replay shows what recording stored per page and per build over the last 7 days, day by day, and the recordings’ share of the storage runway.

  • Daily cap (Settings → Session replay → Recording cost): megabytes the whole instance may store per UTC day. Once reached, recorders stop and no new recording starts until the next day. Replicas see each other’s uploads within about 30 seconds, so the cap can be passed by that much.
  • Sampling: the share of sessions recorded, as a default and per page — an exact pattern such as /content/orders/:id, or a prefix such as /reports/* (the most specific rule wins; 0% never records the page). Each tab decides once per visit, so a page is either recorded or not for that person throughout; while a tab is on a page that is not recorded nothing is kept, and the replay picks up again on the next recorded page.
  • Clips attached to errors are not sampled, but they count toward the cap and stop when it is reached.
  • With @nivaro/react, pass useSessionRecorder({ build }) to name your app’s build; it defaults to the @nivaro/react version.

Older recordings move to storage

Recordings older than 3 days (Settings → Session replay → Storage) leave the database: each one is compressed into a single file in the file storage driver — local disk, S3 or Azure Blob, as set under Settings → File storage — and its rows in the database are removed. An hourly job does the moving; a recording still receiving events is left until it has been quiet for an hour.

  • Opening an older recording loads it back first; the player says “Loading from storage…” for the few seconds that takes. It then stays loaded for 24 hours before the copy in the database is dropped again (the file stays).
  • When the retention period ends, or a recording is deleted, its file in storage is deleted too.
  • DB Health → Session replay shows how much sits in the database (hot) and in storage (cold), and the storage runway counts both.
  • Switching the storage driver does not move recordings already in storage: they are read from the active driver, then from local disk. Moving from one cloud driver to another leaves older recordings unreadable until they are purged.

Health check

While recording or error clips are on, the readiness scorecard runs a Session recording is healthy check. It warns, with the figure and the likely cause, when:

  • more than 5% of chunk uploads failed since yesterday (at least 20 uploads) — refusals the server saw (too large, recording closed or at its size cap) plus failed attempts the recorders report on their next successful upload. A browser that never gets through again cannot report, so the real figure can be higher;
  • no recording started in the last 24 hours while people were signed in (the recorder is blocked, starts are failing, or sampling records nobody);
  • the daily recording cap was reached, naming the page that stored the most that day;
  • the oldest recording is more than a day past the retention period (the daily purge is not running).

Recording your own frontends

Apps built on the headless API record themselves with one hook from @nivaro/react (rrweb is an optional peer dependency — install it in the host app):

import { NivaroProvider, useSessionRecorder } from '@nivaro/react'

function App() {
  useSessionRecorder({ app: 'customer-portal' })
  return <Routes />
}
  • The hook no-ops unless the instance toggle is on AND rrweb is installed — safe to ship always-on.
  • Recordings attribute to the authenticated SDK identity (usually your service token user); the app label tells frontends apart in the replay list.
  • Raw SDK commands exist too: sessionRecordingEnabled, startSessionRecording(app), appendSessionRecordingEvents, endSessionRecording.
  • The hook keeps the same console and network log as the admin recorder (below), from your app’s own fetch and XMLHttpRequest calls.

Error clips work the same in your own frontend: with Error clips on, the hook keeps the last 30–60 seconds in memory and uploads nothing until something breaks. Call reportClientCrash from your error boundary and the issue it files links to the clip (or, with full recording on, to the moment in the live recording):

import { reportClientCrash } from '@nivaro/react'

componentDidCatch(error, info) {
  void reportClientCrash(client, error, info) // POST /issues/client + replay link
}

Support clips: with Error clips on, a support request (Get help, Request a change) cuts the same in-memory buffer into an app='support-clip' recording, taken when the dialog opens and uploaded only if the request is sent; the requester can untick it. POST /session-recordings/start takes clip_kind ('error' | 'support') from an allowlist, so a clip's label is never free text.

Auto-record on a signal

With "Auto-record on signals" on (Session Replays header; nivaro_settings.replay_auto_signals, off by default), trouble starts a short recording even while recording is off: the next three minutes of the people affected, labelled auto:<signal>, inputs masked as always.

  • rage-click — three clicks on one element within 600ms; dead-click — three clicks on buttons or links that changed nothing (no DOM change, no navigation within a second) inside ten seconds. Both arrive with the RUM beacon, sent at once, and record the person who clicked.
  • monitor — an ops monitor flips to failing; breaker — an operator opens a Traffic Map breaker on an entity. Both record the people currently on the pages that show it (/collections/<c>…, /records/<c>…), as seen by the API process that noticed (the page pings of the admin and of portals using usePageAt).
  • The server sends replay:record { signal, minutes: 3, token } over the socket; the token is single-use, minted for that person and that signal, and lives two minutes. POST /session-recordings/start honours an auto start only with it, so a page cannot start one itself.
  • Capped at 12 auto recordings per hour for the instance (counted in Redis across API processes) and one per person per ten minutes; at most ten people per signal.
  • With full recording already on, the signal is only marked on the live recording (a signal tick). With error clips on, the auto recording rides the clip buffer instead of starting a second rrweb stream.
Journey Trail (page breadcrumbs) covers most debugging needs without recording anything visual — reach for replay when you need the pixels.

Timeline markers, console and network

Recordings capture context alongside the pixels: every route change, every console warning and error the page emitted, and a light log of the page’s requests. console.log and console.info are skipped as noise (recordings made before this also kept info lines, and still show them).

  • Console lines are cut to 200 characters, at most 500 per page load. Anything that looks like a credential is replaced with [redacted] before it is kept: JWTs, Bearer and Basic credentials, long hex or base64 strings, and the value of anything named token, secret, password, API key, authorization or cookie.
  • Requests keep the method, the route with ids replaced by :id, the status and how long it took, at most 1,000 per page load. No query strings, bodies or headers; a call to another site keeps its host. A request that never got an answer shows as failed. The recorder’s own uploads are left out.
  • The page’s address in a route marker gets the same redaction, so a reset or invite link’s token is not kept.
  • The player’s scrubber shows the markers as colored ticks — blue for route changes, red for console errors, amber for warnings. Clicking a tick seeks the replay to just before that moment. Info-level console lines are kept out of the scrubber to avoid clutter.
  • Beside the player, a Console / Network panel lists the console lines and requests. The line at the playhead is highlighted, later lines are dimmed, and the list scrolls itself to follow the replay unless your pointer is over it or you have just scrolled it. Clicking a line seeks the replay to it. Console has a filter per level with counts. While you follow a session live, the panel stays open and new lines arrive as the person works; clicking a line then leaves live mode and opens the recording at that moment.
  • On a narrow window, and in the Traffic Map’s Recording level, the panel sits under the player instead.
  • This makes "what was the user doing when that error fired" a one-click question — find the red tick, click it, watch.

The event rail

Under the scrubber, a second row of markers shows what the same person did on the server while the recording ran, from the API log, the issue log, the page trail and workflow history: their requests, client errors they reported, admin pages they entered and workflow transitions they made.

  • Colours: requests grey when they succeeded, amber for a 4xx and red for a 5xx; client errors red; page changes blue; transitions violet.
  • Hover a marker for what it was (method, path, status and time for a request). Markers a few pixels apart merge into one that lists what it holds, so a busy recording stays clickable.
  • Click a marker to seek to just before it. Ctrl-click (⌘-click on a Mac) an error or a transition to open the issue or the record.
  • Requests show method, path, status and duration only, never bodies or query strings. The recorder’s own uploads are left out.
  • A long recording shows at most the first 500 requests, 100 errors, 300 page changes and 200 transitions; hovering the rail says when a kind was cut.
  • Times come from the server’s clock and the recording from the browser’s, so a marker can sit a second or two off the moment on screen.

Clips: select a range

Drag along the thin track under the scrubber to select a range; drag either handle, or focus it and use the arrow keys (Shift for 5 seconds), to adjust it, and Escape to clear it. The strip under the player shows the range and can move either end to the playhead.

  • Raise an issue cuts the range into a replay of its own (labelled clip in the list) and opens a new issue linked to it. The issue says which page the clip opens on, lists the console errors in it and the person’s requests in its window (from the event rail), and adds your note.
  • A clip starts from the last full page snapshot before the range, so it plays exactly what was on screen at its first second. Its events are copied as they were stored: masked inputs stay masked.
  • A clip raised as an issue is kept for the same number of days as any recording.

Clip library

Save clip keeps the selected range in the library with a name, an optional description and tags. Session Replays → Library lists saved clips newest first: search by name, description or tag, filter by a tag, play a clip in place and delete it.

  • A saved clip is a replay of its own, cut from the recording the same way as a clip raised as an issue, with the masking it was recorded with.
  • Retention skips recordings the library holds: the clip stays until someone deletes it, while the rest of the recording it came from expires as usual. Delete clips you no longer need — the library is the one place recordings are kept indefinitely.
  • Saving and deleting clips is recorded in the activity log.

Sharing a replay with one person

Share… on a selected range creates a link for one person you pick, valid for 1 hour to 30 days (3 days by default). They get a notification with the link; you see it once, to copy.

  • Never public: the link opens only for the person it names, signed in as themselves — they do not need to be an administrator. Anyone else signed in gets a refusal, and so does a masquerade session.
  • They see only the shared window, with the masking it was recorded with — not the rest of the recording, its event rail or any other session. The page says who shared it and when the link expires.
  • Every open is recorded in the activity log, and so is every refused attempt. The share dialog lists the links made from a recording: who shared it with whom, the window, the expiry and how often it was opened.
  • Revoke deletes the link at once. A link also stops working when it expires or when its recording is purged by retention — save the range as a clip first if it must outlive the recording.
  • Only a fingerprint of the link is stored, so the link itself cannot be read back from the database.

Search by record or field

As each recording uploads, the server indexes what it touched: the pages visited (with ids replaced by :id), the records opened (collection and id), the names of the fields focused or typed into, and the elements clicked, as selectors. The Search tab on the Session Replays page finds recordings by collection and record id, by field name or by selector, and opens each one at the moment it matched. A record’s Timeline (the History button) links to Replays of this record.

  • Only field names (the data-field a form row carries) are indexed, never what was typed: inputs are masked before they leave the browser, and the index never reads values or page text.
  • Selectors are built from stable hooks only (data-testid, data-field, data-cbv-* and fixed ids), so the same element matches across recordings.
  • Indexing runs after the upload has been answered and never slows it down. Recordings uploaded before the index existed are not searchable.
  • Index rows are deleted with their recording, by retention or by Delete.
  • What went wrong: the Search tab also takes a page and an outcome — a failed request (4xx), a server error (5xx) or an error reported by the browser — within the last day, 7 or 30 days. Each failing request in the API log (or client error report) is matched to the person’s recording that was running at that moment, and the recording opens five seconds before the first failure (GET /api/session-recordings/search?outcome=4xx|5xx|client_error&route=&days=). Request bodies are never shown; a hit lists the method, path and status.

Following one record: search by collection and record id, then Play all. Every recording that opened the record plays as one timeline, oldest first, each cut to the time the person was on the record plus a minute either side. The strip above the player names the person and time of each part; under it, Record as they found it links to the revision in effect when they arrived, and Saved here to any revision saved during that part. When a part ends the next one starts, unless you turn that off; click a part in the strip to jump to it.

Inspecting an element

Pause a replay and click anything in it: the inspector outlines the element and shows its selector (with a Copy button), its data-* attributes, and the nearest data-field and data-cbv-* hooks on it or above it. Find in other recordings lists the other recordings in which someone clicked or typed into the same element, from the replay index; Open in Search shows them all with a Watch button that opens each one at that moment. An element with no stable hook on it or above it gets a plain selector such as button, which cannot be searched for. The inspector reads attributes only, never text or what was typed.

Heatmaps

The Heat tab shows where people click on a route and how far down they scroll, summed over every recording of that route in a date range. Pick a route on the left; the route is drawn as it was last recorded, with the clicks over it, the most-clicked elements and the share of visits that reached each screen beside it.

  • Heat is aggregate-only. A nightly job (session-replay-heat, 02:05 UTC) folds finished recordings into counts per app, route pattern, day and screen size: click positions as 2% squares of the viewport, the element clicked, and the deepest point of each visit. No person, recording or session is stored with the counts, and nothing in them can be traced back to who clicked.
  • Routes are patterns (/collections/workflows/:id), never record ids. Element names prefer test hooks, labels and short button text, and leave out text with digits or addresses, so a record’s data does not become an element name.
  • Each run takes at most 300 recordings (about 250MB stored), oldest first, and marks them folded; a backlog drains over the following nights. Error clips are left out. Run it now from Jobs.
  • The drawing of the route comes from the newest recording that showed it. When that recording has expired with retention, the heat is drawn on a blank viewport instead; the counts themselves are kept for 180 days.
  • Positions are relative to the viewport, so a phone and a wide monitor put the same button in different places. Pick one screen size to sharpen the map.

Frustration score and Worst sessions

Every working session gets a frustration score from 0 to 100. A session is one browser tab’s run of admin pages on one day (the page trail’s session). The Worst sessions tab lists the highest scores in a date range with the person, the route they spent most time on, what made the score and a Watch button when a recording overlaps the session. The People page’s Day view shows the day’s worst score beside its summary; it links to that session’s replay when there is one. Unlike heat, a score is about one person, so every read is admin-only.

  • Rage clicks: three or more clicks on one element within 600 ms (real-user monitoring).
  • Dead clicks: clicks that changed nothing, when the page reports them to real-user monitoring.
  • Client errors: errors the page reported to the issue log during the session.
  • Back-and-forth: page A, then B, then A, then B again within two minutes (the same exact pages; browsing a list and different records is not counted).
  • Slow calls: requests slower than that route’s 95th percentile for the same window (at least 20 calls to judge by) and slower than one second.
  • Abandoned forms: a new record held at least 10 seconds, or an existing record held at least a minute, and left with no save to that collection or record while it was open. A page whose length is unknown never counts.
  • Each signal adds its weight, at most ten of a kind, and the score is 100 × (1 − e^(−sum ÷ scale)), so it levels off toward 100. Defaults: rage 6, dead 3, client error 8, back-and-forth 3, slow call 2, abandoned form 5, scale 25 (one client error scores 27). Change them under Weights on the Worst sessions tab; a weight of 0 turns a signal off. They are stored in settings as frustration_weights.
  • A nightly job (session-frustration, 02:25 UTC) rescores the last two days, so a session that ran past midnight or a late report is picked up. Scores are kept 90 days and are deleted with the person. Run it now from Jobs.

Notes on a recording

Under the player, the Notes list pins a remark to a moment of the replay. A note is pinned to the playhead at the moment you start typing it (click the time chip to re-pin it to where the playhead is now), and shows as a violet flag in a row under the event rail. Click a flag or a note’s time to seek to it.

  • Notes are admin-only, like the recordings themselves, and are shown as plain text. Only the author can edit a note; any admin can delete one. Notes go when the recording goes.
  • Copy a note onto an issue linked to the recording (it lands as a comment on the issue, shown in the issue’s detail) or onto an open investigation notebook from the Traffic Map (appended to its notes). Either way the copy carries a link that opens the recording at that second.
  • Adding, deleting and copying a note are recorded in the activity log.

Exporting a recording

Export (top right of the player) saves a recording outside the admin. Leave From and To empty for the whole recording, or give a window in m:ss.

  • HTML replay: one file with the player and the events inside. It opens offline in any browser and plays like the admin’s player. The events are exactly as stored, so inputs that were masked when recorded stay masked.
  • WebM video: the server plays the recording in a headless browser and captures it in real time, so a video takes as long to make as the window lasts (at most 30 minutes). When it is ready you get a notification with a link to the file; if it cannot be made, the notification says why. The server needs ffmpeg for this.
  • A window starts at the last full snapshot before From, because a replay needs the page as it was; playback still begins at From.
  • Every export is recorded in the activity log. The video is stored as a file owned by you; treat both files like the recording itself, since they show someone’s session.

A Playwright spec from a recording

Export → Playwright spec turns the clicks, typing and page changes in a window of the recording into the E2E recorder’s steps and opens them in the E2E recorder, where you can remove steps, add assertions, type in the values and save the spec into an extension’s tests folder (on a development machine) or download it.

  • Selectors prefer a data-* hook on the element (or the nearest one above it), then role and accessible name, then id, label, name, placeholder and a short CSS path.
  • Typed values were masked when recorded, so they never reach the spec: each one is a placeholder such as <value for data-field="po_number">.
  • A click on an element the recording never captured is left out and counted. Making a spec is recorded in the activity log.

Skipping inactivity

Stretches longer than 5 seconds with no input (mouse, keys, scroll, touch) and no change on the page play at 8×; a stretch that would still take more than a few seconds at 8× is jumped over to its last 2 seconds. The scrubber shades each one with how long it was ("skipped 2m 10s") and a badge over the replay says when it is skipping. The Skip idle / Real time button beside the speeds turns it off; the choice is remembered in this browser.

  • Each recording’s active time — the time between input or page changes, every idle stretch counted as at most 5 seconds — is worked out as its chunks upload and shown on the list ("4m 12s active"). Sort a person’s recordings by Most active to find the sessions where something actually happened.
  • Recordings made before active time was measured show no figure and sort last.

Chapters

A recording splits into chapters at every page change — from the recorder’s own route markers and the server’s page trail, merged when both saw the same navigation. A change of query string alone (a filter, a tab) stays in the same chapter, and a page left within a moment (a redirect) is folded into where it landed. Under the scrubber the chapters are listed with their page and length, the current one highlighted; click one to jump to it, or press , (back) and . (next) while watching.

The list shows how many chapters each recording has, counted from the route markers as the recording uploads (recordings made before this show no count).

Floating player

Float (beside the speeds) detaches the replay into a small window in a corner of the admin, so it keeps playing while you open the record it is about, a drill-down or anything else — moving between admin pages does not stop it. Drag the window by its title bar; it settles into the nearest corner, and that corner is remembered in this browser. A pinned chat panel moves it over instead of covering it. Closing the window takes you back to Session Replays with the replay open at the moment it had reached; the square button stops it without going anywhere. Opening another replay on the Session Replays page closes the floating one.

Watching together

Watch together (under the player) starts a shared viewing and copies its link. Every admin who opens the link follows your playhead: when you play, pause, seek, jump a chapter or change speed, their replay does the same, and a small roster shows who is watching (you lead, with a crown). Copy watch link copies it again; Stop ends it, and closing the replay leaves. A follower can still scrub on their own, but your next move brings them back. If you close the replay while others watch, they can carry on, and one of them can take the lead.

  • Only admins can join, and only on a recording that exists for them; a watch link opens that recording and no other.
  • Discuss posts a link to the current moment — and the shared viewing, when there is one — into one of your chat rooms with an optional note, then opens the room. Copy link in the same menu copies it instead. The link opens Session Replays at that moment (a few seconds before it).
  • It runs over the admin’s live connection: nothing about the viewing is stored.

Health

The Health page at /health (Operations → Health) has three tabs: Status, Monitors (/health/monitors) and Telemetry (/health/telemetry). Status gives a live view of every subsystem, backed by a detailed health endpoint that goes beyond the public liveness probe.

GET /api/health/detailed
{
  "db":        { "ok": true, "latency_ms": 4 },
  "redis":     { "ok": true },
  "migrations":{ "ok": true, "pending": 0 },
  "sockets":   { "connected": 12 }
}

Startup

The page ends with how long this process took to start, phase by phase: migrations, building the server, routes, extensions, scheduled flows, event flows, listening, and the warms that run beside the boot. Each bar sits where the phase began and is as wide as it took. The newest 20 starts are kept per instance; a phase that took at least twice its usual time and a second longer is marked, and so is the whole start.

GET /api/ops-runtime/boot
{
  "instance": "production",
  "total_ms": 5120,
  "usual_total_ms": 4800,
  "slow": false,
  "slow_phases": [],
  "phases": [
    { "name": "Migrations", "ms": 1400, "at": 900, "background": false,
      "usual_ms": 1350, "slow": false }
  ]
}

Probes for proxies and deploys

Four public or admin endpoints answer four different questions. Point each consumer at the one that matches its question.

EndpointQuestionWho calls it
GET /api/versionIs the process alive, and which build is it?Container health check, the redeploy notice
GET /api/readyMay the proxy send this process traffic now?Proxy health check, the deploy gate
GET /api/preflightDid this deploy land coherently?Deploy gate, the Health page (admin)
POST /api/ops-runtime/smoke?strict=1Do reads, writes and extensions work end to end?Deploy gate (admin)

/api/ready answers 200 only when the boot has finished, no migration in this build is pending, every extension named in REQUIRED_EXTENSIONS loaded, the database answers SELECT 1 within 2 seconds and Redis answers PING within 500 milliseconds. It is never “degraded”: a slow dependency fails the check rather than keeping the process in rotation. A process that received SIGTERM answers 503 at once, so the proxy stops routing to it while in-flight requests drain.

GET /api/ready  → 200 or 503
{
  "ready": true,
  "checks": [
    { "id": "boot", "ok": true, "summary": "Boot finished." },
    { "id": "migrations", "ok": true, "summary": "All 384 migrations applied; no files missing." },
    { "id": "extensions", "ok": true, "summary": "All 1 required extension(s) loaded." },
    { "id": "database", "ok": true, "ms": 80, "summary": "Database answered in 80ms." },
    { "id": "redis", "ok": true, "ms": 2, "summary": "Redis answered in 2ms." }
  ]
}

The smoke suite (database, Redis, migrations, collections read, required extensions, a request to the API itself) answers 200 with ok in the body by default, which is what the Ops Console button reads. Add ?strict=1 and it answers 503 when any check fails, so a deploy script can branch on the status code alone.

Which process runs scheduled jobs

With more than one API process, only one fires scheduled jobs. Every process whose ticks are enabled (CRON_TICKS) competes for a lease in Redis; the holder renews it every 10 seconds and releases it on shutdown, so another process takes over within seconds. A process stops believing it holds the lease shortly before the lease could expire, so a Redis outage stops its ticks before anyone else could start. Each scheduled fire also takes its own lock, so one fire runs once even if two processes briefly overlap during a deploy. Run now works on any process and needs no lease. Boot catch-up runs only on the lease holder.

Jobs names the instance that holds the lease. GET /api/job-runs/registry and GET /api/ops-runtime/roster return it as scheduler ({ instance, is_leader, holder, ticks_enabled }). A process with ticks off never competes: run web replicas with CRON_TICKS=off and one worker with it on.

Jobs labelled unsafe to run twice (the digests, broadcasts, chat sends and report deliveries) take a cluster-wide “running” marker in Redis while they run. A second start anywhere, whether run now, a chained run, a boot catch-up or the clock, is refused while the marker is held; run now answers 409 with code JOB_RUNNING and names the holder. If Redis cannot be asked, the run is refused too. The marker is renewed while the job runs and expires five minutes after a process dies.

Heavy jobs take turns across every process through one Redis slot, so a run now on a web replica never runs beside the worker’s nightly heavy job. A heavy job waits for the slot (up to two hours, then runs with a warning); if Redis is down it runs at once. scheduler.heavy_slot names the job holding the slot.

Metrics for Prometheus

GET /api/metrics returns the Prometheus text format for this process: version and instance, memory and CPU, event-loop delay since the previous scrape, request counts and a latency histogram by route pattern (/api/items/:collection, never a raw URL), the database pool (in use, waiting, ceiling, five-minute p95 wait) and whether the process holds the scheduler lease. A scraper reads it with Authorization: Bearer <METRICS_TOKEN>; without METRICS_TOKEN only signed-in administrators can. Scrapes are not written to the API request log.

# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: nivaro
    metrics_path: /api/metrics
    authorization: { credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/nivaro-metrics-token }
    static_configs: [{ targets: ['nivaro-web:3055', 'nivaro-worker:3055'] }]

Secrets from files

Any setting can come from a file instead of the environment. X_FILE=/path sets X from that file (set X or X_FILE, not both). Every file in /run/secrets whose name is an environment-variable name becomes that variable, which is where Docker Swarm mounts a secret under its target name; NIVARO_SECRETS_DIR moves the folder and off turns it off. A secret file replaces a value already in the environment and the log names the variable, never the value. One trailing newline is dropped. An unreadable file stops the process at boot.

GET /api/extensions also carries each extension’s build: the export’s own build value, or else the .release-sha file a deploy writes beside the extension. A deploy gate compares it with the release it mounted.

GET /api/health remains the lightweight unauthenticated liveness check; it reports latency as degraded, so do not use it for routing. The detailed endpoint requires authentication.

Realtime Event Pipeline

When a record changes, open pages hear collection:update with the collection, the record id, the action and the NAMES of the fields written (never a value). This page covers how those events survive a sleeping laptop, a server that lost Redis for a moment, and writes that bypass the items service. Admin → Realtime → Event pipeline shows the counters and the delivery probe.

Catching up after a long absence

Every event carries a sequence number. A client that reconnects sends the last one it saw and receives what it missed. The fast journal in Redis keeps 15 minutes (5,000 events); every event is also written to nivaro_event_journal and kept 24 hours, so a laptop back from a night asleep replays the changes instead of reloading every list. Past 24 hours, or more than 500 events for the pages it has open, the client reloads as before.

Across servers

With several API servers, record-change events travel between them on a Redis stream (nvr:ev:stream), each server reading from its own position. A server that loses Redis briefly picks up where it stopped, so its users miss nothing. Other socket traffic (presence, chat, notifications) still uses the Socket.io adapter. REALTIME_EVENT_STREAM=off restores the adapter for record changes too.

During a rolling deploy from a build without the stream, users connected to an older server miss events from newer servers until that server is replaced; they then catch up from the journal on reconnect.

Changes made outside the API

Batch edits, imports run by a procedure, stored-rollup recalculations and extensions that run SQL announce the records they changed, so open pages refresh. A stored procedure or an outside script reports its changes by writing to the inbox table nivaro_raw_writes; the API reads it every 5 seconds and broadcasts each change with source: "raw".

-- From a stored procedure (SQL Server): comma list of ids, or NULL for "records in this collection changed"
EXEC nivaro_announce_writes @Collection = 'forecasts', @Ids = '101,102,103',
  @Action = 'update', @Fields = 'status,amount', @Source = 'procedure:reforecast'

-- Any database: insert rows directly (item NULL = collection-wide)
INSERT INTO nivaro_raw_writes (collection, item, action, changed_fields, source)
VALUES ('forecasts', '101', 'update', 'status', 'script:fix-lines')

// From an extension
await ctx.sql.announceWrites?.('forecasts', ids, { action: 'update', changed_fields: ['status'] })
  • More than 100 records of one collection in one go become a single event with item: "*" and bulk: <count>: lists show the "new changes" pill and open records refetch quietly.
  • Imports run by a procedure announce the collections listed in their "Recalculate rollups" setting.
  • Only names and ids are broadcast. Pages read the new values through /items, where permissions apply.

Delivery probe

A Realtime delivery monitor (Monitors → New → Realtime delivery) runs every 5 minutes: a test connection inside the server joins a private room, a probe event goes out through the normal path (journal, durable table, stream) and the monitor records how long it took to arrive. Slower than the limit (default 2,000 ms), never arriving, or arriving without being journaled fails the check and raises an issue. "Run probe now" on the Realtime console runs the same check; the last 50 results from every server are kept.

Realtime Load Test

scripts/realtime-load-test.mts opens N simulated Socket.io clients, writes to a throwaway table at a steady rate and reports how long events took to arrive, what each socket costs the server in memory, how much Redis traffic the run caused and how the event stream behaved. Use it before a release that touches the socket layer, or to size an environment.

What it does

  • Creates a throwaway table zz_loadtest_<random> (registered as a hidden collection) and a throwaway active user with an admin role and a static token. Every client signs in with a one-time ws-token minted for that user.
  • Splits the clients across rooms by --mix record/collection/chat (default 20/70/10): collection clients join collection:<table>, record clients sit in one record room, chat clients join a room the user cannot see (it measures the join gate; no chat message is written, because chat tables are real data). Half the clients (--coalesce-share) opt in to merged bursts.
  • Writes alternate creates and updates through /api/items. Delivery latency is the time from sending the request to the collection:update arriving, in two groups (clients that receive every change, and clients that receive merged bursts, whose latency includes the one-second merge window), plus the arrival time relative to the write response. One record client sends a record:signal per second; its latency is reported apart.
  • Memory is the RSS change of the target process (--api-pid) between before the clients connect and after they have joined, divided by the sockets. Redis traffic is the INFO stats delta of commands and bytes over the run. Stream lag is read from /api/realtime/pipeline every two seconds.
  • In finally, and on Ctrl-C, it deletes the rows the API wrote about the table (activity, revisions, journal), the metadata rows, the table, the user and the rows that name the user, then checks and prints that they are gone.

Smoke run (shared development database)

The development database is shared with staging, so the default mode refuses anything but 127.0.0.1:3132 and caps a run at 200 sockets, 5 writes per second and 60 seconds. Start a throwaway API on that port with its own Redis channel prefix, and no migrations or crons:

cd api
SKIP_BOOT_MIGRATIONS=1 CRON_TICKS=off PORT=3132 REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX=lt: npx tsx src/index.ts
# in another shell (use the pid of the node process that listens on 3132)
cd api && npx tsx ../scripts/realtime-load-test.mts --api-pid <pid> \
  --sockets 200 --ramp 8 --rate 5 --duration 40 --out /tmp/rt-load.json

Full scale (dedicated environment only)

A real capacity test needs thousands of sockets and a sustained write rate, which belongs on an environment with its own database and Redis, never the shared one and never a deployed host. Run the API there with the production settings you want to size, run the script from a separate machine (one Node process holds a few thousand sockets: raise ulimit -n, and run several copies at once if you need more, adding their results), and lift the smoke limits explicitly:

npx tsx scripts/realtime-load-test.mts --target https://loadtest.internal:3055 \
  --full-scale --confirm-dedicated loadtest.internal:3055 \
  --sockets 5000 --ramp 120 --rate 50 --duration 600 --out rt-5000.json
  • --confirm-dedicated must equal the target host and port; it is the only thing between the script and a database that real people use.
  • --api-pid only works against a process on the same machine; against a remote API read the process memory from your monitoring and divide by the connected sockets (server_socket_count in the report).
  • Redis figures are whole-server deltas: run on a Redis nothing else uses. On two or more API nodes, stream.delivery_lag_ms fills in (a single node reads back its own entries and reports own_skipped_delta instead).
  • Watch for: collection_loss_pct above zero (events not delivered), a rising delivery_lag_ms or stream_len_after over the run, connect times growing with the ramp, and RSS that does not level off after the clients disconnect.

Reading the report

FieldMeaning
connectionsClients that signed in, connect time p50/p95/p99, drops and connect errors
writesWrites sent and failed, HTTP time of the write itself
deliveryUpdates received against expected (clients in the collection room times writes), latency per client group, record-signal latency
memoryRSS before and after connecting, in KB per socket
redisCommands and bytes during the run, stream length before and after
streamEntries published and delivered, publish failures, delivery lag samples
cleanupWhether the throwaway table, metadata rows and user are gone

Presence Load & Stall Alerts

A busy morning can stall the API without a single error: every open tab refetching the online list on every presence event keeps each process's JavaScript thread at 100%, the event loop lags by seconds, socket events arrive late and requests queue. Two tools cover it: a repeatable load script shaped like real signed-in browsers, and three monitors that fire while it happens.

The presence load script

scripts/realtime-load.mjs opens N signed-in browser sessions against a target API. Each person keeps one tab, or two (--two-tab-share, default 0.6: 250 people ≈ 400 sockets), and each tab behaves like the app today: its own socket (signed in with a one-time ws-token, in the user_presence collection room), a presence ping every 15 s, a presence-row heartbeat every 25 s, an idle flip now and then, an occasional reconnect, and a refetch of /api/presence/online on every presence event (joining a fetch already in flight). It never creates users or business data: sessions sign in with the tokens you give it, and the only writes are the ones an open tab makes about itself.

node scripts/realtime-load.mjs --target https://staging.example.com \
  --allow-shared-host staging.example.com \
  --tokens-file ~/load-tokens.txt --admin-token "$ADMIN_BEARER" \
  --people 250 --ramp-minutes 10 --steps 5 --hold-minutes 5 --out rt-250.json

# what it would do, without opening anything
node scripts/realtime-load.mjs --target http://127.0.0.1:3099 --people 250 --dry-run
  • **Tokens**: --tokens a,b, --tokens-file (one per line), REALTIME_LOAD_TOKENS, or one --api-key. View-as tokens (nvm_…) make every session a different person; one API key looks like one person with many tabs. Tokens are reused round-robin when there are fewer than people.
  • **Ramp**: --start 0 --people 250 --ramp-minutes 10 --steps 5 adds people in five steps and prints one row per step (people, sockets, req/s, online-list p95, delivery p95 and share within 2 s, missed events, server event-loop lag, pool used and waiting, the generator's own lag), then holds the full load for --hold-minutes. The row where lag climbs is the capacity edge.
  • **Server figures** come from GET /api/ops-runtime/runtime (administrator bearer: --admin-token), sampled twice every 5 s so a load balancer spreads them across processes; each process is reported by host.
  • **Delivery latency** is measured from each presence write (idle flip, heartbeat) to every tab that receives its event; a coalesced event delivers several writes at once. Sampled events are acknowledged like real clients, so the delivery SLO sees the run too.
  • **Client fixes**: --refetch-debounce-ms 2000 models a debounced online list, --refetch off none; compare runs to size a fix before shipping it.
  • **Refusals**: no default target; a host whose name says prod or production is always refused; this checkout's PUBLIC_URL / ADMIN_URL / DB_HOST and TRAFFIC_REPLAY_SHARED_HOSTS need --allow-shared-host <host> naming them exactly; over 300 people needs --confirm-scale <host>.
  • One machine holds 400 sockets comfortably. If the generator lag column passes ~200 ms, its own latency figures are suspect: lower --max-inflight or split the run across two machines.

Stall, rate-jump and per-node delivery monitors

Three monitor types on Health → Monitors (**New monitor**). They are off until an administrator creates one, run every 5 minutes with the other monitors, and a failing flip raises an issue and notifies the creator and subscribers. Every API process publishes its own figures to Redis every 30 seconds, so the process that runs the monitors judges all of them — including the web processes that serve the traffic.

MonitorFails whenDefaults
Event-loop stallAny API process peaked above the lag limit in that many of 5 consecutive minutes (searched over the last 9 minutes, so a stall between two runs is caught). A lone GC pause never fires.1000 ms, 3 of 5 minutes
Route rate jumpA route (all processes together) runs at that many times its own trailing hour and above the floor for 2 minutes in a row, while its share of all requests at least doubles. The share rule keeps a morning sign-in wave quiet: everything grows together. An optional ceiling fails any route above it.5×, 20 req/s, share ×2 — sized for ~250 people (≈120 req/s in total)
Delivery by nodeAny process delivers fewer than the target share of realtime events within the SLO time over the last 15 minutes (probe and real browsers' acknowledgements). The overall SLO can look fine while one process lags.The SLO targets (95% within 2 s), 20 samples minimum
  • Config keys: event-loop threshold_ms, breach_minutes, window_minutes; route jump factor, min_rps, sustain_minutes, share_factor (0 = off), min_history_minutes (processes younger than this stay out of the comparison), ceiling_rps; delivery window_minutes, min_samples, target_ms, good_pct.
  • Route templates come from the route definition (GET /api/items/:collection), never raw ids.
  • Cloud mode: all three answer "unknown" — process figures are shared by every tenant on a process and are not kept per tenant.

Database

The Database page at /database (Operations → Database) has four tabs: Overview, Tuning (/database/tuning), SQL checks (/database/sql-checks) and Redis keys (/database/redis). Overview is a read-mostly console over the database server, Redis, and the API process itself. Every endpoint behind it is admin-only. Panels that need database-server visibility degrade honestly: if the database login lacks the VIEW SERVER STATE permission, the panel shows an amber note saying exactly that instead of failing.

What the panels show

PanelWhat it tells you
This processUptime, memory, event-loop lag, and connection-pool usage for the replica that answered — per process, not fleet-wide.
Instance rosterEvery live API replica registered in Redis (empty when Redis is down).
Cache consoleIn-process caches on this replica, each with a Bust button (and a bust-all). Every bust is audit-logged.
Degradation mapWhat stops working when each dependency (database, Redis, SMTP) goes down. Database and Redis are probed live.
Top expensive SQLThe 15 statements costing the server the most CPU since its last restart. SELECT statements get an Explain button that opens the query plan.
DeadlocksRecent deadlock events mined from the server health session, with the statements involved.
Long transactionsSleeping sessions that have held an open transaction idle for 5+ minutes.
Unused indexesNonclustered indexes with heavy writes and zero reads since the server last restarted.
Table heatRead/write activity per table since the server last restarted.
RedisMemory, clients, keys, hit/miss counters, evictions.
Storage runwayDatabase size now, a daily growth rate from nightly snapshots, and the largest tables.
Held connectionsChecked-out pool connections attributed to the request holding them — the leak finder.
Data velocityWhich collections are being created/updated the most, from the activity log.
Latency by hourSlowest routes by hour of day (UTC) over the last 7 days.
Dangling foreign keysRegistered relations whose FK values point at rows that no longer exist, with guarded repair actions.
Redundant indexesAn index whose key list is a strict prefix of another index on the same table — it answers nothing the wider one cannot and taxes every write. Filtered and unique coverers are never counted as covering. Drop goes through the same guarded path as unused indexes.
Backup tablesScratch copies a one-off fix left behind (zz_…, …_backup, …_bak): row count, size, age and the last time anything read them. Only tables that are not registered collections and that no foreign key references are listed; rows older than BACKUP_TABLE_STALE_DAYS (default 30) read amber.

The write actions, and their guardrails

  • Drop an unused index — only plain nonclustered indexes qualify: the server re-checks the index at drop time and refuses primary keys, unique indexes, and clustered indexes outright. Every drop is audit-logged with the index name. Remember the usage counters reset when SQL Server restarts, so "zero reads" on a recently restarted server is weak evidence — check the uptime first.
  • Kill a long transaction — requires a typed reason (the KILL button stays disabled without one), only works on user sessions (session id above 50), and refuses to kill the console’s own connection. The reason lands in the audit log alongside the session id.
  • Drop a backup table — two clicks, and only a table the listing itself returned qualifies: the listing is the allow-list, so a registered collection or a table some foreign key points at can never be dropped from here, whatever the name looks like. The drop is audit-logged with the row count and size it held.
  • Dangling-FK repair offers two actions only: null out the broken reference (refused on NOT NULL columns) or delete the orphaned rows through the normal delete path, so trash, deletion guards, and hooks all apply. Repointing to a different record is deliberately not offered.

Environment Config — what drifted since

The config-snapshot job stores a gzipped snapshot of every configuration table each night at 04:40. Secrets are stripped from every snapshot — by a list of known credential columns and by name (any column named like a secret, password, token, API key, private or access key or credentials), so a column a later migration adds is dropped too; a snapshot stored before a column joined the list is stripped again whenever it is read. Environment Config → **What drifted since…** picks any stored snapshot and compares the live rows against it with the same engine the file upload uses — added, removed and changed rows per table, field by field. Snapshots identical to the one before are dimmed: a run of identical hashes is the answer "nothing drifted". **Store a snapshot now** takes one on demand. API: GET /config-diff/history, POST /config-diff/history, GET /config-diff/since?id=|at=.

Environment Config — restore points

Every stored snapshot is also a **restore point**: an undo for a bad layout, pipeline, permission or settings change that a full database restore would be far too blunt for. Records are never touched — only configuration tables.

KindStoredKept
NightlyThe config-snapshot job, 04:40Newest 30
Manual**Store a snapshot now**, or POST /config-diff/historyNewest 10
Before migrationAt boot, when at least one migration is pending — names the migrations about to run. The whole step is time-boxed (PRE_MIGRATION_SNAPSHOT_MS, default 30 s, 0 = off); a snapshot that runs out of time stores nothing and boot continues. Replicas booting together store one (an application lock; a replica that finds it held skips).Newest 10
Before deployThe deploy script: POST /config-diff/history {"trigger": "pre-deploy", "version": "<new version>"} (admin; takes as long as a snapshot, ~30–60 s)Newest 10
Before restoreJust before a restore writes — only the tables that restore touches. Restoring it undoes the restore.Newest 10

Retention is per kind, so thirty nightly snapshots never push the last deploy's restore point out. Only manual and pre-deploy may be sent by a client; any other trigger answers 400.

Restoring

  • **Restore config to this point** previews every config table the snapshot carries: per table how many rows come back (deleted since), change back (edited since) and are removed (added since), with the rows and the changed fields. Untick tables to restore fewer, then preview again.
  • The apply is bound to the preview: it recomputes the plan, then inside the transaction takes an application lock (one restore at a time, across servers), re-reads the touched tables with update locks and compares again. When live configuration changed since you previewed it writes nothing and shows the new preview (409 STALE).
  • One transaction for the whole restore — all of it or none. Rows keep their ids. Deletes run child-first and inserts parent-first along foreign keys; a row that still cannot be written (a record or a table outside the restore references it) rolls everything back and names the row. A statement waits at most 10 s for someone else's lock, then the restore stops with nothing written (409 LOCKED).
  • At most 2,000 changed rows per restore — untick tables to restore a bigger difference in parts.
  • Grants to people — User Scopes, owner-group members and team members — come back only for people who are active now; grants to someone suspended, redacted or a placeholder are left out and counted in the preview.
  • When removing a row would also delete or clear rows in other tables through a foreign key (a queue takes its items and sources with it), the preview lists them and the restore stays disabled until you tick **Also delete or clear those rows**.
  • Before writing, a **Before restore** point of the touched tables is stored; the result panel links to it as **Undo this restore**.
  • Never restored: people accounts (nivaro_users), sign-in providers, each person's own pins, column choices and subscriptions, chat memberships and learned AI playbooks. Secret columns are stripped from snapshots, so a restore never overwrites a live secret; a row that differs only in columns added after the snapshot is left alone.
  • Caches are flushed, other replicas follow the configuration number, and open forms pick up the change. Each restored table gets a config-restore activity entry.

API (admin): POST /config-diff/history/:id/restore {mode: "preview"} → {plan_hash, tables[], refused[], totals, warnings}; {mode: "apply", plan_hash, tables?, allow_cascade?} → {pre_restore_id, tables[], totals}; preview also returns cascade[] and totals.skipped_inactive_user. The single-table apply from an uploaded snapshot (POST /config-diff/apply) uses the same engine: upsert only, the same refused tables and grant rule, and mode: "apply" needs the preview's plan_hash.

Layout drift

Every layout mutation snapshots the state before it, so the newest version against the current rows is exactly **what the last save changed**. Table Editor → Version history shows that diff first and any version's diff on demand (assignments keyed by field, since the save route re-inserts rows; groups by id), with warnings for the shapes that meant damage before — column widths nulled wholesale, slot flags flipped off together, half the fields gone. The readiness check layout-drift sweeps every layout for those shapes. API: GET /collection-layouts/:id/versions/:v, …/versions/:v|newest/diff?against=current|<v>, GET /collection-layouts/drift.

Custom queries — used by, and procedure shape

The query editor's **Used by** card lists everything that references the query by slug or id — page widgets, record widgets, report widgets and catalog presets, metric and anomaly definitions, flow operations, other queries. Below it, **Procedure shape** checks each INSERT … EXEC in the wrapper against the procedure's real first result set: INSERT … EXEC binds by position, so the declared column COUNT must equal what the procedure returns; names are shown but never fail the check. SQL Server cannot describe a procedure that builds temp tables inside — those read "cannot be described", and the last failing run on this process (a shape error) is the honest fallback. The readiness check custom-query-shapes runs the same comparison over every wrapper. A **Temp tables** card below it lists every #temp the wrapper builds and whether it is dropped first (IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#x') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #x or DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #x before the build): a batch that fails between CREATE and DROP leaves the table on the pooled connection, and the next wrapper on that connection dies "There is already an object named #x". The same readiness check warns on every enabled wrapper with an unguarded temp table. API: GET /custom-queries/:id/dependents, GET /custom-queries/shape-report.

Dead columns

Columns a model change left behind are registered in api/src/db/dead-columns.ts with the date the last writer stopped, what replaced them and whether they can be dropped yet. pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run dead-columns:check greps every source tree and fails when code still names a column marked droppable; the readiness check dead-columns reports droppable columns still present on the database (the dropping migration has not run there) and lists what still blocks the retiring ones. GET /ops-db/dead-columns is the same view. Migration 336 dropped the first one, the queues table's retired view-mode column.

Open transactions on the pool

A stored procedure that opens a transaction without SET XACT_ABORT ON and then fails leaves the transaction open: the batch stops, the connection goes back to the pool mid-transaction, and the next caller on that connection inherits it. Every raw EXEC path now rolls an open transaction back on the same connection before releasing it (custom queries, rule exec_procedure actions, long-running statements), and the readiness check proc-transaction-guards lists every procedure with BEGIN TRAN that carries neither SET XACT_ABORT ON nor a CATCH that rolls back.
