People already signed in keep working: a session never calls the identity provider. Someone signing in is sent back to the sign-in page, which says the provider is not answering. It never shows a raw error, and it never sends them back to the provider in a loop.

Chaos Results

Every chaos drill ends with a report, and the reports add up to a scorecard: which claims about how Nivaro degrades are proven, which broke, and which nobody has checked lately. All of it is for administrators and stays readable on instances where drills cannot run.

Run report

Open a finished run from the Runs tab (Full report) or go to /chaos/runs/<id>. While the run is still going the same address shows the live cockpit.

  • The verdict: held, broke or aborted, and the limit that broke it.
  • One chart per limit, before, during and after the fault, with the normal range from before the drill, the limit line, and the alerts and notes marked where they happened.
  • Time to detect: from arming the fault to the first alert, the first "noticed" note or a declared incident.
  • Time to fix: to the first "fixed" note.
  • Time to recover: from the end of the fault until every limit was back inside its normal range. "Not back while watched" means the samples after the fault never returned to it.
  • The alerts that fired, what the readiness checks said, and the errors people actually saw: server errors by route (ids removed), client error reports and rage or dead clicks, as counts only.
  • The participants’ notes and the full timeline.

Copy link gives a stable address other administrators can open. Export postmortem downloads the report as Markdown (timeline, figures and notes, never record data) to paste into a postmortem.

Claims and the matrix

The Matrix tab shows every dependency (the database, Redis, the file share, each partner API, the AI gateway, sign-in, sockets and mail) against the ways it can fail: down, slow, errors and cut off. Each cell takes the colour of its newest drill and fades as that drill gets older; an outlined cell has never been proven. Click a cell to open its last report or run it again with the start form already filled in.

Under the matrix, Claims lists what Nivaro says about degrading (for example, "when Redis is unreachable, requests keep answering") with the drill that last proved each one. A claim is proven when its newest drill held within the last 30 days, stale when that drill is older, broke when its newest drill broke or stopped itself, and never proven when nothing has run. A fault proves a claim when it names the claim in its catalog entry.

The readiness check "Resilience claims are proven" warns when a claim is stale or its last drill broke. Claims never proven are listed but do not warn. It is skipped where drills cannot run (cloud, or production without CHAOS_ENABLED).

Trends

The Trends tab shows median time to detect and time to recover per month or quarter, a calendar of the days drills ran (Eastern dates; an outlined day had a drill that did not hold), each dependency’s verdicts month by month, and the claims never proven. The strip on top (the last 90 days) is also served as JSON for a recovery-time panel.

API

RouteReturns
GET /api/chaos/runs/:id/reportThe run, its report, errors people saw, actor names and the share link
GET /api/chaos/runs/:id/postmortemThe report as a Markdown download
GET /api/chaos/claimsEvery claim with its status and last run
GET /api/chaos/matrixRows, fault kinds and one cell per pair with its last verdict and re-run spec
GET /api/chaos/trends?months=12Monthly and quarterly timings, drills per day, verdicts per dependency, never-proven claims and the recovery feed

Chaos game days

A game day is a planned drill: a date and time, the people taking part, and a timed list of things that will go wrong. It lives on the chaos console (Operations → Health → Chaos) under Game days. Chaos is refused in cloud mode and on production unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true, so game days are for staging and development.

Planning a day

  • Plan a game day opens the editor. Start from a blank plan or the monthly staging template (kill a web task, drop Redis, block the file share, slow the database, with checkpoints before and after).
  • Times are Eastern. The length is 15 minutes to 8 hours.
  • People: a lead (faults are armed as the lead), an optional scribe, and responders. Everyone named gets an invitation at once and reminders 24 hours and 15 minutes before (notification category "Chaos drills and game days").
  • Injects run at +mm:ss after the start: arm a fault from the catalog for a number of seconds, post an announcement to the day’s channel (as the lead, through the normal chat send), or reach a checkpoint. A fault key this instance does not have is a warning when you save and is skipped on the day.
  • Chat channel: a private channel for the participants. A timeline bot posts each fault and checkpoint as it happens, with fixed wording only — never the plan’s own labels. Start a huddle from the channel header.
  • Repeat monthly: when the day ends or is cancelled, the same slot next month (same weekday, same week of the month, same Eastern time) is planned with the same people.

On the day

  • The lead presses Start now, or the scheduler starts the day at its time when "Start automatically" is on. Each fault inject goes through the drill pre-flight; a refusal is recorded on the timeline instead of stopping the day.
  • Injects fire on time from the chaos-gamedays job (every minute, one server) and from a timer on the server that started the day; whichever comes first fires it, and it fires once. An inject more than ten minutes late is marked missed and never fired late.
  • Fire now runs a waiting inject by hand. End day closes the day, stops any fault still armed and writes the result; Abort does the same with the verdict aborted. Stop all on the console always works and ends a running day too.
  • The day’s verdict is the worst of its fault runs (held, broke or aborted).

Scribe marks

While a day runs, anyone taking part can stamp what happened in one click — Noticed, Found cause, Fixed — or type a note. The marks become the day’s time to detect, time to find the cause and time to fix, measured from the first fault that went live, and show on the inject track and in the report. Notes stamped on one of the day’s fault runs land on the day itself.

Blind mode

  • A blind day hides its faults from the responders: no drill banner for them, and drill-tagged alerts are not marked as a drill for them. The lead and chaos operators (administrators) still see everything.
  • Declare incident (Ops Console header) is open to everyone signed in. It stamps a "Declared incident" mark on every running game day and blind drill — the responders’ time to detect — and always answers the same way, so it never gives away that a drill is running.
  • The lead reveals the drill at any time; the faults then show on the banner for everyone and the channel gets a line saying so. A single drill can also be started blind through POST /api/chaos/blind/runs.

Killing a web task

The API never writes to Docker. The "Kill a web task" fault queues the host runbook chaos-kill-web-task in the Runbooks host queue; the host agent on the swarm manager runs it and swarm replaces the task. A deployment declares that runbook in its extension (runs on the host, no dry run needed, a target such as staging). Without it the fault is refused with that reason. Stopping the fault withdraws a kill still waiting in the queue.

API

RouteWhoWhat
GET /api/chaos/gamedaysadminEvery game day
GET /api/chaos/gamedays/:idadminPlan, timeline, fault runs, people, time to detect / fix
GET /api/chaos/gamedays/activesigned inThe days I take part in (titles and times only)
POST /api/chaos/gamedayschaos operatorPlan a day; PATCH /:id edits it while planned
POST /api/chaos/gamedays/:id/start | step | end | cancel | revealchaos operatorRun the day; step takes {inject_id}, end takes {how}
GET / POST /api/chaos/runs/:id/notesadmin or participantScribe marks {mark, text}
POST /api/chaos/declaresigned inDeclare incident
POST /api/chaos/blind/runschaos operatorOne drill, blind; /blind/runs/:id/reveal reveals it

Operators, Limits, Monkey & Phone Stop

Four things keep chaos drills safe in day-to-day operations: who may run them, how far a run may reach on each instance, a Chaos Monkey that runs small drills at random times when you switch it on, and a Stop button that reaches your phone.

Chaos operators

Administrators may always run faults. In **Chaos → Settings** an administrator can name roles whose members may also start, stop and record drills (and read the chaos console). Only administrators change these settings, so an operator can never widen their own reach. API keys limited to named collections are refused. Only administrators may override the working-hours pre-flight check.

Limits on this instance

Each instance keeps its own limits, so development and staging can differ even when they share a database. The server applies them to every run started there — from the console, a game day, Chaos Monkey or a script — whatever the form sent.

LimitWhat happens over it
Faults allowedA fault off the list is refused (403 CHAOS_CAP).
Share of trafficA larger share is lowered to the limit. A run aimed at everything becomes that share when the fault can take a share; any other target (some routes, a table, a person, a replica) is sampled at the limit on top. A route pattern with fewer than two fixed parts (/*, /api/*) is refused.
Added delayEvery delay measured in ms is lowered to the limit.
Run lengthThe window is shortened (never under 5 seconds).
ReplicasA run that would reach more replicas is narrowed to the one it started on, or refused when the fault cannot aim at one replica.

Whatever was lowered is recorded on the run (meta.caps). Empty means no limit beyond the fault’s own.

Socket drills started from the Realtime page (/realtime → Verification) are the one path outside these limits and the pre-flight: they are administrator-only, pass the same gate, and keep their own 5–600 s window and share/room/person targets. Stop all on the Chaos page ends them too. Start a socket drill from the Chaos console (fault “Socket drill”) when you want the limits, the pre-flight and a run with a verdict.
Stored under the chaos key of this instance’s nivaro_settings_overrides row (GET/PATCH /api/chaos/settings, administrators). No migration.

Alerts during a drill

An alert that fires while a fault is armed — log alert rules, request rules, monitors, metric alerts, integration alerts, a readiness check turning to fail — is never silenced or rerouted: everyone who normally hears about it still does, by every channel they normally get. Its message gains a line naming the run: “May be caused by the chaos drill …” when the alert is about what the fault touches (a database alert during a database fault), otherwise “Fired during the chaos drill …”. The drill’s people (whoever started it, the game day’s lead, scribe and responders; for Chaos Monkey, administrators and chaos operators) are told too, in-app, when they were not already. The Ops Console, Telemetry and the Integrations console show a **Drill** tag on alerts that fired during a run. In a blind game day the note is left out of the normal recipients’ copy; the alert itself still reaches them.

Chaos Monkey

Off until an administrator turns it on in **Chaos → Monkey**. Every 15 minutes, inside the days and hours you set (Eastern time), it may start one drill from the faults you approved, at random moments so that about the weekly number land across the week. Each drill is small (a share of traffic, else one replica) and short, and the instance’s limits apply on top. Administrators and chaos operators are told when it starts and when it ends, with the verdict.

  • Never on an instance that looks like production (its instance key, or NIVARO_TIER=production), and never while another drill is armed.
  • Pre-flight still judges every drill (deploys, maintenance, open incidents…); a refusal is kept as a refused monkey run and does not count toward the week.
  • **Try now** runs one tick at once, skipping only the dice.
  • The chaos-monkey job ticks only where scheduled jobs run, on one server at a time.

Stop from your phone

When a drill starts, and again if it stops itself because what should stay true broke, the person who started it and its participants get a browser notification with **Stop all faults**. Tapping it ends every fault on the instance, even when that phone is not signed in.

The button carries a signed token that works once, only for that person and run, and only until the drill’s window ends (five minutes after an abort). The person must still be a chaos operator. It keeps working while Redis is down and during maintenance.

Browser Chaos & Pretend Down

Browser chaos mode makes **your own tab’s** requests fail or slow down for a few minutes, so you can watch how screens cope: error messages, retry buttons, autosave and the offline outbox. Nothing is injected on the server and nobody else is affected.

Available to administrators when the server allows chaos drills (GET /api/chaos/status). It is refused in cloud mode and, on a production server, unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true. When the server has no chaos route the controls do not appear at all.

The chaos toolbar

Open it from your user menu → **Browser chaos**, or press **⌘ Shift .** (Ctrl Shift . on Windows) anywhere. Pick what breaks, how hard and for how long, then Start. While it runs, a pill in the bottom-right corner shows what is on and the time left; its × stops it at once.

PresetWhat your tab sees
Flaky networkA share of requests (5–90%) fail as if the network dropped them; the rest arrive late.
API downEvery API call answers 503, as a proxy does when no API server is behind it.
Slow APIEvery API call waits longer (0.25–10 s).
OfflineRequests fail as if the network is gone, and the browser reports itself offline, so the offline banner and outbox take over.
Socket goneLive updates stop; at the end the tab reconnects and reloads what it missed.
Fail my next savesThe next N creates, edits or deletes answer 500. Reads keep working. Combines with any preset or runs on its own.
  • It always ends on time (1 to 30 minutes). A reload of the tab keeps it on until then; closing the tab ends it.
  • Signing in and out, the chaos controls themselves and the error reporter are never broken.
  • Crash reports sent while chaos is on are marked and not filed as issues.
  • With several tabs open, live updates come over one shared connection: Socket gone silences only this tab, the others keep theirs.

Pretend down in design mode

While designing a dashboard or a form, you can see how it looks when something it depends on fails. On a dashboard use **Pretend down** in the header; in the layout editor (and a record page’s Edit layout) open **Preview** and use the Pretend down list at the bottom.

  • The list names what the view uses: the data behind each group of dashboard widgets, a form’s record widgets and panels (pipeline, owners, comments, tasks…), the AI gateway, partners and external APIs, and live updates.
  • Switch one on and the widgets that use it fail through their normal error handling, so you see exactly what a person would see.
  • Only your tab, only while the editor is open. Leaving the page turns everything back on.
  • The Preview button says how many things are pretended down, so it is never on unnoticed.

In a custom front end

Headless front ends built on @nivaro/react get the same tools. Call installClientChaosFetch() first thing at boot (before anything creates an SDK client), mount <ClientChaosToolbar user={me} /> once, and add clientChaosAxiosInterceptor(AxiosError) to any axios instance. Sockets created through createWorkerSocket or createSocketRealtime are covered automatically; call bindClientChaosSocket(socket) for any other.

import { installClientChaosFetch, ClientChaosToolbar } from '@nivaro/react'

installClientChaosFetch() // before anything creates a client

<ClientChaosToolbar user={{ is_admin: me.is_admin }} />

Chaos on the Traffic Map

Where chaos drills are allowed (never in cloud mode; on production only with CHAOS_ENABLED=true), the Traffic Map shows every armed fault on the nodes it acts on, so nobody reads a drill as a real outage. Where chaos is refused, nothing here appears.

Armed faults on the map

A node a fault acts on is hatched in red with a dashed outline, and a label names the fault and the time it has left (the soonest to end, plus how many more). The edges into a faulted database, Redis, email or partner node are dashed. The toolbar shows the drill and links to its run; selecting a hatched node lists the drills acting on it, with Open run.

The fault acts atDrawn on
Every request, a share or one replica (http.request)Every API lane
Routes matching a patternThe entities whose routes match
One personThat person on the callers side
The database (db.*), or one tableSQL Server, and that table’s entity
Redis (redis.*)Redis
Email, SMS, push (mail.*, sms.*, push.*)That channel
Partner calls (external.*)Every partner node
File storage, AI providersFile storage, each AI node
Socket drillsThe Sockets lane
The scheduler (cron.*)The scheduled job nodes

Inject fault here

Right-click a node, or use the inspector’s action row, for Inject fault here. It opens the chaos console on the Faults tab with that fault’s start form already aimed at the node: a route pattern for an endpoint or a lane, the table for a collection with a database fault, the person for a caller, everything for a data store, a channel or a partner. Nothing starts until you press Run there. Socket drills open the Realtime page’s own drill form.

The same right-click menu offers Simulate down on a dependency: what would break if it went away, worked out from recorded traffic, with nothing switched off (see Traffic Map: Act).

The console link is /chaos?tab=faults&fault=<fault key>&target=<kind>:<value>, for example target=route:/api/items/orders* or target=table:orders. A target the fault cannot take is ignored and the form opens with its usual default.

Chaos Drills Outside the App

Four scripts in scripts/chaos/ prove recovery behaviour that cannot be tested from inside a running API: booting without the database, a lock left by a dead migration, links that slow down or drop, screens that meet a failing API, and a deploy that runs while people are using the system. Each one prints PASS or FAIL per check, always writes a JSON result file, and with --record <base-url> (and an admin token in CHAOS_RECORD_TOKEN) posts the run to the chaos console.

None of these may be pointed at production or at the shared development database. They start their own throwaway API or database, or (the deploy drill) measure a staging deploy you start yourself.

Boot and migration recovery

pnpm chaos:boot starts a throwaway API twice, once with the database unreachable and once with Redis unreachable (closed local ports) and a short BOOT_DEPS_WAIT_MS. A pass means the process logged its retries with backoff and exited 1 inside the window, which is what lets the orchestrator restart it cleanly. It also runs the unit test that proves a migration lock held past MIGRATION_LOCK_STALE_MS is freed and the migrations then run.

With CHAOS_SCRATCH_DB=<database> set to a scratch database (never an EFP_ database) the script also holds knex's lock row there, boots with migrations and MIGRATION_LOCK_STALE_MS=15000, and expects the "Freeing the stale lock" line and a live API. Run it before every release that touches the boot path.

Resilience tests with toxiproxy

deploy/chaos-ci/docker-compose.yml runs SQL Server, Redis, the API image and toxiproxy; the API reaches the database and Redis through toxiproxy and the test runner reaches the API through it too. pnpm chaos:toxiproxy adds latency, resets, timeouts and outages and checks: boot under database latency, concurrent reads under latency all answer, a database outage turns /api/ready to 503 and recovers without a restart, a session survives a Redis blip, and a socket reconnects and signs in again after its connection is reset.

  • CI: .github/workflows/chaos-ci.yml runs it on pull requests that touch the database layer, plugins, server.ts, boot code or realtime.
  • Locally: docker compose -f deploy/chaos-ci/docker-compose.yml up -d --build --wait api, then node scripts/chaos/toxiproxy-suite.mjs. --mode host runs the API from your checkout instead of the image; --only db-outage,socket runs chosen cases.
  • SQL Server does not run under emulation on Apple silicon. Run the suite in CI or on an x86 host.

Error-state gallery

pnpm chaos:gallery opens admin screens in a browser at 1440 px, light and dark, while every /api call is answered by a mock: a 500 with a realistic error body, a request that never answers, or no network at all. It screenshots each one and writes reports/error-gallery/<date>/index.html (not committed) with a filterable grid and summary.json. --sample 15 (default) picks evenly spaced routes, --all walks every route, --routes /a,/b picks some. --start-admin starts a throwaway admin dev server for you.

FlagMeaning
blankThe main area has no text at all.
raw-errorStack, axios or "[object Object]" text is visible.
stuck-loadingA spinner or skeleton is still showing 10 seconds in.
no-error-shownA request failed and the screen shows content or an empty state without saying so.
page-errorAn uncaught exception reached the page.
error-boundaryThe crash screen appeared.

A pass is a gallery with no flags. The point is a list to work through, and a re-run per release to see it shrink.

Rolling deploy under load

pnpm chaos:deploy-load measures a deploy; it never starts one. Staging only. Run it with --target <staging url> --token <bearer> --caller <k12|u<uuid>>, then start the deploy the usual way. It replays a slice of recorded traffic (traffic:replay, which keeps its own refusals) while polling /api/version and /api/ready every 250 ms, and once the version changes it keeps measuring for --after-s seconds. --load builtin --rps 20 uses a simple generator instead of a recorded slice.

It reports "this deploy dropped N of M requests", how many more answered 5xx, how long two versions answered together, the longest stretch with nothing ready, and how long one socket took to reconnect. A pass is nothing dropped and nothing errored. --dry-run proves the counting on a throwaway API that restarts itself, so it is expected to show drops.

Let AI do this — tasks and support tickets

The person a task or a support ticket is assigned to can ask AI to do it for them. The model reads — as that person, with their permissions and scopes — the task title and description, the record it sits on, the thread and the request type, and answers with one of three things: a plan, a few questions it needs answered first, or “AI can’t do this” with the reason and a manual checklist. A plan is an ordinary Ask AI plan: every step is validated and previewed as the assignee, nothing changes until they approve it, and it shows up in Plans history like any other.

Off until an administrator turns it on — Settings → AI Features → Let AI do this, separately for tasks and for support tickets. Only the assignee (or their active delegate) sees the button; an administrator sees it only on work assigned to them.

Where the button is

  • A record’s Tasks panel and the Tasks slot on a layout — the sparkle icon on each open task of yours.
  • My Work → My tasks — the same icon on every row.
  • Support → Desk → a ticket’s detail — “Let AI do this” beside Pick it up.
  • The panel opens beside the button. “Draft a plan” asks the model; it takes a few seconds and counts toward the daily cap.

Reviewing the plan

Above the steps the panel shows an estimated run time (from how long recent plans took per step kind, or a stated default rate), the hands-on time AI thinks it saves (labelled as its estimate), and a risk level — low, medium or high — from the records changed, steps that cannot be rolled back (notifications, chat posts, flows, tasks), deletes and how many collections it writes to. Steps that cannot be rolled back are called out before you approve. Under each step: the records and fields it touches (old → new where the preview has them), the people it tells, and whether it calls other systems or may email.

  • Remove a step, or change a value where the step kind allows (the fields an update writes, a message’s subject and text, a task’s title). The step is rebuilt and previewed again as you.
  • “Ask for a different plan…” sends a note back; the current draft is discarded and a new one drafted.
  • Approve & run all, run step by step, or Run later (a scheduled plan is re-checked first). Progress is live; a failed step stops the plan and offers Re-check and retry.
  • When the plan changes more records than the threshold (default 50), a second person — the task’s creator, else an administrator — must approve it first. They are notified; Approve & run opens once they have.

When it finishes

  • One summary comment lands on the task or ticket thread as you — every step’s outcome and a link to the plan. A ticket’s requester hears about it the way they hear about any reply; nothing else is sent.
  • “Mark task done” / “Mark ticket done” closes it; on a ticket, “Draft reply to requester” writes a reply from the outcome for you to edit and send through the normal reply box. Nothing is sent on its own.
  • “Undo what AI did” — for seven days after it ran (administrators always, from Plans) — shows what will be restored and what cannot be (sent notifications, chat posts, flows), then restores it. A record someone edited since is shown and left alone; newer edits are never overwritten. The rollback is noted on the thread and in the task history.

Settings and analytics

SettingWhat it does
On tasks / On support ticketsEach off by default.
Roles that may use itNothing ticked = every role.
Support request types that allow itNothing ticked = every type.
Second approval aboveRecords a plan may change before a second person must approve. 0 = never.
Drafts per person per dayHow many times one person may ask per day. 0 = no limit.

Plans → History shows administrators a “Let AI do this” card: plans drafted from tasks and tickets in the last 90 days, how many ran, were rejected or rolled back, how many wait for a second approval, and the hours AI estimated it saved. Every model call is in the AI call log under the feature task-do.

API

RouteWhoWhat
GET /api/ai/task-do/meanyoneWhich kinds this person may use.
GET /api/ai/task-do/tasks/:idtask’s peopleAccess verdict + this task’s plans.
POST /api/ai/task-do/tasks/:id/draftassignee{answers?, note?, previous_plan_id?} → {kind: plan | questions | cannot}.
GET /api/ai/task-do/plans/:idowner, approver, adminThe plan with review figures.
POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/editowner{remove_step} or {set: {step_id, field, value}}.
POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/approvecreator / adminThe second approval.
POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/draft-replyownerTicket: an AI-drafted reply (not sent).
GET / POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/undoowner (7 days), adminPreview, then restore.
GET / PATCH /api/ai/task-do/settingsadminThe settings block.
GET /api/ai/task-do/analyticsadminThe card’s figures.
